questions.title: Deadlock Storm Under Load: Root Cause and Prevention
questions.prompt: Your OLTP system is throwing an increasing number of deadlock errors (1205) during peak hours, and the on-call team's current fix is just to retry the failed transaction. As the architect, walk through: what a deadlock actually is at the lock-manager level, why SQL Server resolves it by picking a victim, and the concrete, durable design changes you'd make to drive the deadlock rate toward zero rather than just making retries cheaper.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock is a circular wait: Transaction A holds a lock Transaction B needs, while B simultaneously holds a lock A needs, so neither can ever proceed without intervention. SQL Server's lock monitor periodically scans for exactly this cycle and, once found, picks a 'victim' to roll back automatically, based on which transaction is cheaper to undo (or an explicit DEADLOCK_PRIORITY setting), raising error 1205 to the victim's caller. Retrying the rolled-back transaction only treats the symptom — it does nothing to reduce how often the cycle forms in the first place. The durable fixes are architectural: (1) enforce a consistent access order to tables across every code path that touches them, since the single most common real-world cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; (2) keep transactions as short as possible, moving validation and unrelated reads outside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary so locks are held for the minimum necessary time; (3) review indexing so transactions acquire narrow row/page locks instead of escalating to page or table locks on large scans, which dramatically widens the blast radius of any single transaction; (4) consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT isolation, which removes most reader/writer blocking entirely via row versioning, at the cost of additional tempdb version-store overhead; (5) for cases where natural ordering genuinely can't be enforced, use sp_getapplock to serialize access explicitly. Before declaring any fix complete, capture an actual deadlock graph (via Extended Events' xml_deadlock_report) to confirm the real access pattern rather than guessing from symptoms.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team, respectfully, that retrying is a band-aid, not a fix — it just hides the real cost of the problem. First I'd pull an actual deadlock graph, not just the error count, because I want to see exactly which two statements and which two resources are colliding before I propose anything. Nine times out of ten it comes down to two code paths touching the same tables in opposite order, so step one is standardizing access order across every stored procedure that touches those tables. Step two is auditing transaction length — anything that's validating data or doing unrelated reads inside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary comes out. Then I look at whether lock escalation is widening the blast radius because of missing indexes, and only after that do I bring up snapshot isolation as a structural option, being upfront that it moves the cost into tempdb rather than eliminating it. I'd present this as 'here's the mechanism, here's the evidence, here's what actually gets the rate toward zero' rather than just 'add a try/catch and retry.'
commonMistakes: Treats retry logic as the fix instead of eliminating the cause
Doesn't look at actual access order across stored procedures
Ignores lock escalation thresholds on large updates
Assumes deadlocks are a bug SQL Server should prevent rather than a resolvable mutual-wait
Never captures an actual deadlock graph (XML) before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Defines deadlock as a circular wait on locks, not a generic error
Explains SQL Server's victim-selection mechanism
Identifies inconsistent access order as the most common root cause
Proposes shortening transactions and reviewing indexing to reduce lock footprint
Considers snapshot isolation as an architectural lever, with its tradeoff (tempdb/version store)
Recommends instrumentation (deadlock graph / extended events) before declaring a fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains deadlock mechanics and victim selection
Identifies root-cause patterns (access order, long transactions, lock escalation)
Proposes durable architectural fixes, not just retry logic

questions.title: Reporting Queries Are Blocking the Nightly Order Pipeline
questions.prompt: Business users running ad-hoc reports against the live OLTP database during business hours are intermittently blocking order-entry transactions, and vice versa. Compare the architectural options — read-committed snapshot isolation, a reporting replica, and query hints like NOLOCK — and recommend what you'd actually implement, including what you give up.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, readers take shared locks and writers take exclusive locks, so reports and order-entry transactions genuinely contend for the same locks on the same rows, causing exactly this symptom. NOLOCK (or READ UNCOMMITTED) removes that blocking by skipping locking entirely, but it allows dirty reads, can double-count or miss rows during a page split, and is unacceptable for anything a finance or operations team relies on for correctness — I would not recommend it as a general answer here. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI), enabled at the database level, gives readers a transactionally consistent versioned snapshot from tempdb's version store instead of taking shared locks, so reporting reads stop blocking writers and vice versa, with zero application code changes for ordinary SELECTs — the cost is additional tempdb space and I/O for the version store, and a small per-row overhead on writers. A reporting replica (an Always On readable secondary, log shipping, or replication) solves a different, broader problem: it isolates the reporting workload's CPU and I/O consumption from the OLTP instance entirely, not just lock contention, at the cost of replication lag and additional infrastructure to maintain. My recommendation: enable RCSI first as the fast, low-risk fix for the specific symptom described (lock contention), and treat a readable secondary as the real architectural answer once the reporting workload itself starts consuming OLTP compute/I/O capacity, not just locks. The two aren't mutually exclusive — a mature design often has both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate this into two different problems that look the same from the outside: lock contention, and resource contention. For the immediate symptom — reports and order entry fighting over row locks — I'd recommend turning on read-committed snapshot isolation. It lets readers work off a versioned snapshot instead of taking shared locks, so the blocking just stops, and it needs no code changes. I'd be upfront that it's not free — it adds load to tempdb's version store — but that's a much safer tradeoff than reaching for NOLOCK, which I'd actually argue against here, because dirty reads on order data are a real correctness risk, not just a theoretical one. If the real issue turns out to be that reporting is also eating CPU and I/O the OLTP system needs, that's a different conversation — that's when I'd bring in a readable secondary, because RCSI doesn't give you more hardware, it just removes lock contention. I'd frame it to the client as 'quick structural fix now, workload separation as the next step if reporting keeps growing.'
commonMistakes: Recommends NOLOCK as a general-purpose fix without flagging dirty-read risk
Doesn't distinguish lock contention from resource (CPU/IO) contention
Treats RCSI as free, ignoring tempdb version-store cost
Proposes a replica without acknowledging replication lag implications for 'real-time' reports
keyPoints: Explains why READ COMMITTED causes reader/writer blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and correctly rejects it for anything requiring correctness
Explains RCSI's row-versioning mechanism and its tempdb cost
Recommends a readable secondary/replica as the durable architecture for resource isolation
Distinguishes lock contention from compute contention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the locking behavior causing the blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and its risks accurately
Explains RCSI/snapshot isolation mechanism and cost
Recommends and justifies an appropriate architecture (replica vs RCSI)

questions.title: Parameter Sniffing: One Cached Plan, Two Very Different Row Counts
questions.prompt: A stored procedure filters orders by @CustomerID. For a customer with a handful of orders it returns in milliseconds; for your biggest customer with several million rows, the exact same procedure call times out. Nothing about the query changed. Explain what's actually happening at the plan-cache level, and lay out the durable fixes you'd choose between, including the tradeoffs of each.
questions.modelAnswer: This is parameter sniffing: when a stored procedure compiles, SQL Server peeks at the actual parameter value supplied on that first call and builds one cached execution plan optimized for that value's estimated row count, then reuses that same plan for every subsequent call regardless of what parameter comes in next. If the plan was compiled against a small customer, the optimizer chose a plan shaped for a small result set — likely nested loops with a lookup — and that same plan is catastrophic against a customer with millions of rows, where a hash or merge join with a full scan would have been far cheaper. The symptom isn't random; it's entirely a function of which value happened to compile the plan, which is why it looks like it 'used to work.' Durable fixes, in order of how I'd actually choose: (1) OPTION (RECOMPILE) on the statement forces a fresh, value-specific plan on every execution — correct for every call, but pays the compilation cost every single time; (2) OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR @CustomerID UNKNOWN) uses the average-distribution estimate instead of sniffing any single value, avoiding the worst-case outlier plan but possibly making the common case slightly less optimal; (3) WITH RECOMPILE at the procedure level has the same cost profile but applies to the whole procedure; (4) query store plan forcing lets you pin a known-good plan once identified, needing ongoing monitoring since data growth can eventually make the forced plan wrong too; (5) splitting the procedure into a small-customer branch and a large-customer branch avoids a single plan ever having to serve both distributions. I'd pick based on call frequency and skew.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it the same way I'd explain it to the team that paged me: the procedure didn't change, the data behind one parameter value did, and the plan cache is still serving a plan that was shaped for a tiny customer. SQL Server only looks at the parameter value once, on the first compile, and then it's locked in until something invalidates that plan. So the fix isn't 'optimize the query' — the query's fine — it's deciding how we want the optimizer to handle that skew going forward. For something called rarely, I'd just slap OPTION (RECOMPILE) on it and move on. For something hot, I don't want to recompile constantly, so I'd reach for OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN first, and if I need something more surgical, I'll go find a known-good plan and force it through Query Store, which I'll then keep an eye on, because a forced plan isn't a fix I set once and forget.
commonMistakes: Describes the symptom without naming the plan-cache mechanism causing it
Jumps straight to adding an index without addressing the single cached plan root cause
Recommends OPTION (RECOMPILE) everywhere without weighing per-call compilation cost on hot paths
Doesn't mention Query Store plan forcing as an operational option
Treats the fix as permanent without noting data growth can make it wrong again
keyPoints: Correctly explains that one parameter value's estimate shapes the cached plan for all future calls
Distinguishes RECOMPILE from OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN
Mentions Query Store plan forcing as a monitored, surgical fix
Considers call frequency and data skew when choosing between the options
Notes that any chosen fix needs to be revisited as data distribution changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the parameter-sniffing / plan-cache mechanism
Presents multiple durable fixes (RECOMPILE, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, Query Store forcing, branching)
Weighs the real tradeoffs rather than naming one fix blindly
Chooses between fixes based on call frequency / skew

questions.title: Diagnosing a Job That Shuffles 40 Million Rows Into Eight Wildly Uneven Partitions
questions.prompt: A nightly Spark job joins a 40-million-row transactions table to a dimension table on customer_id, then aggregates. The Spark UI shows the job spends most of its wall-clock time on a single task out of 200, while the other 199 finish in seconds -- and that one task's input partition is roughly 100x larger than the rest. Explain what's actually happening at the shuffle level, why it's specific to this join, and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: This is data skew in the join key, not a resource problem. Spark's shuffle for a join hash-partitions both sides by the join key, sending every row with the same customer_id to the same partition/task -- that's the whole mechanism, and it means if one or a few customer_id values account for a disproportionate share of the 40 million rows, every one of those rows lands in the same single task regardless of how many total partitions you've configured, while the other 199 tasks handle the genuinely distinct, evenly-spread keys and finish quickly. More executors or memory won't fix this, because the problem isn't total capacity, it's that one task has 100x the work of the others. The first thing to check is Adaptive Query Execution's skew join handling (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled), which detects oversized shuffle partitions at runtime and automatically splits them -- this requires no code change and should be tried before anything manual. If AQE doesn't catch this specific pattern, the manual fix is salting: add a random sub-key to the skewed value(s) on the fact side, explode the dimension side so a matching row exists for every possible salt bucket of that key, and join on the composite key -- this spreads the hot key's rows across many tasks instead of one. Diagnosing this correctly means actually looking at the Spark UI's per-task shuffle read size before proposing a fix, not guessing from wall-clock time alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd say is: don't add executors yet. A single straggling task out of 200 while everything else finishes in seconds is the signature of data skew, not insufficient capacity, and throwing more compute at it won't touch the one task that's doing 100x the work. I'd go to the Spark UI stage detail and confirm the shuffle read size on that task before I say another word, because I want evidence, not a guess. Then I'd try AQE's skew join setting first, since it's a zero-code-change flag that handles a lot of these cases automatically now. If that doesn't resolve it, I'd explain salting to the team as 'we're giving the one overloaded key a bunch of fake sub-identities so Spark spreads its rows across many tasks instead of jamming them all into one' -- and I'd be clear we only need to do that for the specific hot key, not the whole dataset.
commonMistakes: Assumes the slow task is a resource/executor problem and just adds more executors
Doesn't check the Spark UI's task-level shuffle read size to confirm it's actually skew
Jumps straight to manual salting without first trying AQE's built-in skew join handling
Salts every key uniformly instead of targeting just the known skewed value(s)
Confuses this with a broadcast-join sizing problem when the dimension table isn't actually the issue
keyPoints: Correctly identifies data skew in the join key as the root cause
Explains hash-partitioning mechanics of the shuffle and why skew creates one oversized partition
Diagnoses using Spark UI task/shuffle metrics before proposing a fix
Proposes AQE skew join handling and/or manual salting appropriately
Considers isolating and broadcast-joining a small known hot key set

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses data skew as the cause, not a resource problem
Explains shuffle/hash-partitioning mechanics accurately
Proposes AQE skew handling and/or salting correctly
Demonstrates proper diagnostic approach using Spark UI metrics

questions.title: A Report That Used to Run in Seconds Now Times Out
questions.prompt: A monthly sales report query against a now-50-million-row fact table has quietly gone from 2 seconds to over 3 minutes as the table grew. Nobody changed the query. Explain, at an architect level, the full diagnostic sequence you'd run to find the cause, the category of root causes you'd expect at this scale, and show the SARGable rewrite for the single most common offender you'd check first.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd run a fixed sequence, not guess. First, turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and look for a scan where a seek should be, and for a large gap between estimated and actual row counts, which flags stale statistics. Second, capture a baseline with SET STATISTICS IO and TIME ON so I have real logical-reads and CPU numbers before touching anything. Third, audit every WHERE and JOIN predicate for non-SARGable patterns — a function wrapping a column, an implicit data-type conversion, or a leading wildcard — because this is the single most common cause of a query that 'used to be fine' degrading purely from table growth: a full scan that was negligible at a few hundred thousand rows becomes minutes of work at 50 million, with nothing about the query's logic having changed. Fourth, check statistics freshness directly via sys.dm_db_stats_properties, since the auto-update threshold scales with table size. Fifth, consider parameter sniffing if the query is parameterized. In this scenario the leading suspect is almost always a non-SARGable date predicate, which I'd rewrite as a range against the untouched column.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never start by guessing or by reaching for 'let's just add an index.' I turn on the actual plan first and look for a scan where I'd expect a seek, and I check the gap between estimated and actual rows, because that gap alone often tells me stale statistics are at least part of the story. Then I capture STATISTICS IO and TIME so I have a real before number. At that point I go straight to the predicates — in my experience, a function wrapped around a column or an implicit conversion is the single most common reason a query that used to be fine quietly degrades as a table grows past tens of millions of rows. I'd show the before-and-after rewrite side by side so it's obvious the fix is removing the function from the column, not adding an index that a wrapped predicate wouldn't even use.
questions.example:
-- Non-SARGable (the likely offender)
SELECT SUM(f.SalesAmount)
FROM dbo.FactInternetSales AS f
JOIN dbo.DimDate AS d ON d.DateKey = f.OrderDateKey
WHERE YEAR(d.FullDateAlternateKey) = 2013;

-- SARGable rewrite: untouched column, range comparison
DECLARE @StartDate DATE = '2013-01-01', @EndDate DATE = '2014-01-01';

SELECT SUM(f.SalesAmount)
FROM dbo.FactInternetSales AS f
JOIN dbo.DimDate AS d ON d.DateKey = f.OrderDateKey
WHERE d.FullDateAlternateKey >= @StartDate AND d.FullDateAlternateKey < @EndDate;
commonMistakes: Jumps straight to 'add an index' without checking the plan first
Doesn't establish a STATISTICS IO/TIME baseline before changing anything
Overlooks stale statistics as a cause distinct from bad predicates
Assumes the query degraded because 'the server is slow' instead of profiling
Adds an index without removing the non-SARGable wrapper that prevents the index from being used anyway
keyPoints: Lays out a repeatable diagnostic sequence: plan, STATISTICS IO/TIME, predicate audit, stats freshness
Identifies non-SARGable predicates as the most common cause at scale
Produces a correct SARGable rewrite
Explains why the same predicate 'got worse' purely from table growth
Mentions parameter sniffing/stale stats as secondary suspects

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a complete, ordered diagnostic approach
Correctly identifies non-SARGable predicates as the leading cause at scale
Provides a correct, working SARGable rewrite
Covers secondary causes (stats, parameter sniffing)

questions.title: Training Data Governance Beyond Data Quality Rules
questions.prompt: A stakeholder says, "We already have data quality rules on our warehouse tables — isn't that enough to cover AI governance for the models we train on that data?" Explain what training data governance covers that traditional data quality does not, and why provenance and consent recordkeeping specifically matter once that data is used to train a model.
questions.modelAnswer: Traditional data quality asks whether a value is accurate, complete, timely, and consistent for its original operational purpose — a customer's address being correct for shipping, say. Training data governance asks a different set of questions on top of that: where did this data legally and ethically come from, did the people or entities it describes consent to it being used for this purpose, is the data representative enough across subgroups that a model trained on it won't encode a skew, and can we reproduce exactly which rows, in which state, trained a specific model version. A dataset can pass every standard quality rule — no nulls, correct formats, timely — and still be governed improperly for AI if it was scraped without usage rights, collected under a consent scope that didn't cover model training, or is systematically under-representative of a population the model will make decisions about. Provenance recordkeeping matters because when a regulator, auditor, or incident review asks 'what data trained the model that denied this loan,' you need a traceable answer down to the dataset snapshot and version, not just 'our warehouse.' Consent recordkeeping matters because data collected for one stated purpose (e.g., fraud detection) being repurposed for another (e.g., marketing model training) without re-consent is a real legal and reputational exposure distinct from any quality defect.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them quality and AI governance are answering different questions, and conflating them is exactly how gaps get missed. Quality rules check whether the data is correct for its original job. Training data governance checks whether we're allowed to use it for this new job, whether it represents the population fairly, and whether we could reconstruct the lineage if someone challenged a model's output a year from now. I've seen a dataset that was spotless on every quality dimension still be a governance problem because it was collected under a consent notice that only covered the original operational use, not model training. So my answer to the stakeholder is: keep the quality rules, they're necessary, but they're not sufficient — we need a separate provenance and consent layer that travels with the data specifically because it's feeding a model, not just a report.
commonMistakes: Treats data quality and training data governance as the same discipline
Doesn't distinguish 'correct value' from 'permitted use' and 'representative sample'
Ignores consent-scope mismatches between original collection purpose and model training use
Can't explain why provenance matters beyond 'it's good practice' — misses the audit/reproducibility angle
keyPoints: Distinguishes data quality (correctness for original purpose) from training data governance (permission, representativeness, traceability)
Explains that quality-clean data can still be an AI governance violation
Covers consent-scope mismatch as a concrete failure mode
Explains why provenance/lineage must be reproducible down to the dataset version used for a specific model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes data quality from training data governance
Explains the consent/provenance-specific risks accurately
Gives a concrete example of quality-clean but governance-non-compliant data
Communicates clearly to a non-technical stakeholder

questions.title: What a Model Card Actually Needs to Say
questions.prompt: Your organization is about to ship its first model card for a production credit-risk model. A product manager asks why you can't just attach the model's accuracy metric and call it done. Explain what a model card is for, what it must document beyond a single aggregate metric, and why that documentation carries real operational and legal weight.
questions.modelAnswer: A model card exists to let someone who did not build the model — an approver, an auditor, a downstream team integrating it, a regulator — understand what the model does, where it's safe to use, and where it isn't, without having to read the training code. A single aggregate accuracy number actively hides the information a model card exists to surface: it says nothing about intended use and out-of-scope use (was this approved for credit decisions only, or is someone about to repurpose it for hiring?), nothing about the training data's provenance and time period, and critically, nothing about performance broken out across subgroups — a model can hit 92% overall accuracy while performing meaningfully worse for one demographic or income band, and an aggregate number buries exactly that disparity a credit-risk model is most legally exposed on. A complete model card documents: intended use and explicit out-of-scope uses, a summary of training data (sources, time range, known gaps), performance disaggregated by relevant subgroups, known limitations and failure modes, and the evaluation methodology itself so results can be reproduced or challenged. This documentation carries legal weight because in a dispute or regulatory inquiry, 'we had a model card documenting the intended use and its known limitations' is a materially different position than 'we had an accuracy number.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on 'attach the accuracy number' directly, because that's the one piece of the model card that tells us the least about where this thing is safe to use. What I actually need documented is intended use — specifically what this model is approved for and, just as importantly, what it's not approved for, because models get repurposed by well-meaning teams who don't know the original scope. I need the training data summarized, including its time range and where it came from, because a credit model trained on data from a different economic period is a real risk. And I need performance broken out by subgroup, not blended into one number, because a credit decisioning model that's quietly worse for one group is exactly the kind of thing that turns into a regulatory or reputational problem months later. The model card is what lets someone who didn't build this model make an informed decision about using it — one number can't do that job.
commonMistakes: Treats a single aggregate metric as sufficient documentation
Omits intended-use and out-of-scope-use statements, enabling later model misuse
Doesn't disaggregate performance by subgroup, hiding fairness gaps
Fails to document training data provenance and time range
Doesn't connect documentation gaps to real legal/regulatory exposure
keyPoints: Explains the purpose of a model card as cross-audience communication, not just a metrics report
Lists required sections: intended use/out-of-scope use, training data summary, subgroup performance, limitations
Explains why an aggregate metric can hide subgroup disparities
Connects documentation completeness to legal/regulatory defensibility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the purpose and audience of a model card correctly
Lists the required content beyond a single metric, with justification
Explains the subgroup-performance disaggregation issue clearly

questions.title: Why AI Lineage Is Harder Than Data Lineage
questions.prompt: Your data lineage tooling already traces a column from source table to dashboard. A colleague assumes that's sufficient lineage for your ML models too. Explain what AI lineage has to capture on top of ordinary data lineage, and why missing any one link in that chain creates a real governance gap.
questions.modelAnswer: Ordinary data lineage answers 'which source columns fed this output,' and that mapping is largely static — a dashboard field maps back to a table and transformation that doesn't change meaning from one query to the next. AI lineage has to answer a much larger set of questions: which exact snapshot of training data (not 'the table,' but the specific version/timestamp of it) trained this specific model version, which feature engineering code and parameter values transformed raw data into model inputs, which hyperparameters and training code version produced this model artifact, which approval and evaluation results that model version carried, and at inference time, which specific input record produced which specific prediction, so a disputed decision can be traced back to the exact model version and the data that shaped it. The reason a missing link matters more here than in ordinary data lineage is that models are retrained and redeployed far more often than warehouse schemas change, so without capturing training-data-snapshot-to-model-version-to-deployment-to-prediction as one connected chain, you cannot answer basic audit questions like 'was this specific adverse decision made by the model version that passed fairness review, or an earlier one that didn't.' Standard data lineage tools generally stop at the feature store; AI-specific lineage has to pick up from there through the model registry and out to the serving layer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct that assumption carefully, because it's a common and costly one. Ordinary lineage tells you a column's path through pipelines — useful, but it stops being useful the moment you ask 'which version of the model made this specific prediction, and what data trained that version.' AI lineage has to connect four things that data lineage tools were never built to track together: the exact training data snapshot, the feature transformation and hyperparameters, the resulting model version and its approval record, and finally the specific prediction a model version produced for a specific input. If any one of those links is missing — say we know the model version but not which training snapshot built it — we can't actually answer an auditor's question about a disputed decision, we can only gesture at it. That's the practical reason I push for lineage tooling that's explicitly AI-aware rather than assuming the existing data catalog's lineage graph already covers it.
commonMistakes: Assumes standard data lineage tooling automatically covers models
Omits training-data-snapshot-to-model-version traceability
Doesn't connect lineage gaps to concrete audit failure scenarios
Forgets that inference-time (prediction-to-input) traceability is part of the chain, not just training-time lineage
keyPoints: Explains what standard data lineage captures versus what AI lineage must additionally capture
Names the specific chain: training snapshot, feature transform/hyperparameters, model version, deployment, prediction
Explains why models change far more frequently than schemas, raising the stakes of a broken link
Gives a concrete audit scenario that fails without full AI lineage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes data lineage scope from AI lineage scope

questions.title: Translating Responsible AI Principles Into Enforceable Controls
questions.prompt: Leadership has approved a one-page 'Responsible AI Principles' statement — fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety — and expects it to actually change how models get built and shipped. Explain how you translate a principle like 'fairness' into something enforceable rather than aspirational, using at least one principle as a worked example.
questions.modelAnswer: A principle becomes enforceable only once it's decomposed into a specific, measurable control with an owner and a gate in the process — otherwise it's a value statement everyone agrees with and nobody is accountable to. Take fairness: the enforceable version isn't 'be fair,' it's a defined set of fairness metrics (e.g., demographic parity difference or equalized odds, chosen deliberately for the use case, since different metrics can conflict) computed against named protected or sensitive attributes, with a documented acceptable threshold, evaluated at a mandatory gate before a model can be promoted to production, with the evaluation results attached to the model card and a named reviewer (not just the model's own author) who signs off. The same pattern applies to the other principles: transparency becomes a model card and explainability requirement with a defined minimum content standard; accountability becomes a named model owner and an approval workflow with a decision log; privacy becomes a specific data minimization and consent-scope check run before training data is approved for use. The common thread is that each principle needs: a measurable proxy, a threshold or rule, a point in the workflow where it's checked, and an accountable role — without all four, the principle stays aspirational no matter how sincerely it's written.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell leadership the one-pager is a necessary first step but it doesn't change anything by itself — what changes behavior is turning each principle into a specific gate with teeth. For fairness specifically, I wouldn't leave it at 'be fair' — I'd pick concrete fairness metrics appropriate to the use case, set a threshold, and make passing that threshold a required step before a model can be promoted, with the results documented and a named approver who isn't the model's own builder. I'd do the same translation for every principle on that page: transparency becomes a documentation standard that's actually checked, accountability becomes a named owner and a sign-off log, privacy becomes a specific pre-training data check. If I can't point to where in our pipeline a principle gets checked, by whom, and what happens if it fails, it's not a control yet, it's a slogan — and I'd rather tell leadership that plainly now than let the program look complete when it isn't.
commonMistakes: Leaves principles as aspirational statements without a measurable proxy
Doesn't name a specific fairness metric or acknowledge that different fairness metrics can conflict
Omits the gate/workflow checkpoint where the control is actually enforced
Doesn't assign an accountable owner distinct from the model's builder
keyPoints: Explains the general pattern: metric/proxy, threshold, workflow gate, accountable owner
Works through fairness as a concrete example with a named metric and threshold
Applies the same translation pattern to at least one other principle
Distinguishes aspirational principles from enforceable controls clearly

questions.title: Choosing Between AI Risk Management Frameworks
questions.prompt: Your organization needs to pick a structural basis for its AI governance program and keeps hearing two names — the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 — without a clear sense of how they differ or whether you need to choose only one. Explain what each framework actually provides, how they differ in nature, and how an organization typically uses them together rather than picking one.
questions.modelAnswer: The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary risk-management guidance framework, organized around four functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — that gives an organization a structured vocabulary and process for identifying and treating AI-specific risks (bias, robustness, explainability, privacy) without being a certifiable standard; you can't be 'NIST AI RMF certified,' you adopt it as a methodology. ISO/IEC 42001 is a management-system standard, structured like ISO 27001 for information security, defining the organizational requirements for an AI management system — policies, roles, risk assessment processes, continuous improvement — and an organization can seek third-party certification against it, which matters for vendor due diligence and contractual requirements in a way a non-certifiable framework cannot satisfy. In practice they're complementary rather than competing: NIST AI RMF is commonly used as the risk-assessment methodology and shared vocabulary that feeds the actual risk register and controls, while ISO/IEC 42001 provides the overarching management-system scaffolding (documented policies, management review cycles, audit trail) that an organization can be certified against, with NIST's risk functions mapped into ISO's required processes. An organization doesn't choose one over the other so much as decide whether it needs certifiability (ISO/IEC 42001) in addition to a sound risk methodology (NIST AI RMF), and most mature programs end up using both, often alongside domain-specific regulation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd clear up the biggest misconception first: these aren't two competing ways to do the same thing, they're different categories of document. NIST AI RMF is a risk-management methodology — it gives you Govern, Map, Measure, Manage as functions to organize your thinking, but nobody gets 'certified' in it. ISO/IEC 42001 is a management-system standard you can actually get audited and certified against, the same way companies get ISO 27001 certified for security. So my recommendation is usually: use NIST AI RMF as the practical risk-assessment engine, because it's genuinely useful for structuring how you think about model-specific risks, and build your management system — policies, roles, review cadence — around ISO/IEC 42001 if certifiability matters to your customers or regulators. I'd tell the organization they're very likely going to end up using both, not choosing between them, and the real work is mapping NIST's risk functions into the process structure ISO 42001 requires.

Doesn't know ISO/IEC 42001 is certifiable and NIST AI RMF is not
Can't describe NIST AI RMF's four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage)
Doesn't explain the practical reason an organization would want certifiability

Correctly characterizes ISO/IEC 42001 as a certifiable management-system standard

questions.title: Data Mesh Governance: What Changes When Ownership Moves to Domains
questions.prompt: A platform engineering leader describes an upcoming move to a data mesh architecture as "basically the same governance, just with the tables living in different places." Explain why that understates what actually changes, specifically what 'federated computational governance' means in a mesh and why domain-owned data products require a different governance mechanism than a centrally-owned warehouse.
questions.modelAnswer: In a centrally-owned warehouse, governance is largely a matter of one team defining and enforcing standards directly on data it also operates — classification, quality rules, and access control are applied by the same group that controls the pipelines. In a data mesh, ownership of the data itself moves to the domain teams that know it best, which means governance can no longer be 'enforced by the people who run the data' because the central governance function doesn't run the data anymore — it has to be enforced through policy that domains implement independently. That's what 'federated computational governance' specifically means: a small set of global, non-negotiable rules (e.g., every data product must carry a classification, an owner, a documented SLA, and pass a minimum quality bar before publication) are defined centrally but enforced computationally — through automated policy checks, platform tooling, and CI-style gates — at the point each domain publishes its data product, rather than through a central team manually reviewing or gatekeeping every dataset. The governance mechanism has to change because the old one assumed a single point of control; a mesh deliberately removes that single point of control in exchange for domain ownership and speed, so without automated, platform-enforced policy, 'federated' governance degrades into no governance at all — every domain making its own ad hoc decisions about classification, quality, and access with nothing holding them to a shared standard.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on 'basically the same governance' because the actual mechanism of enforcement is what's changing, not just where the tables sit. Today, the team that owns the pipeline can also enforce the governance rule, because it's the same team. In a mesh, the domain that owns a data product is not the governance team, so if governance stays 'someone manually reviews this,' it either becomes a bottleneck that defeats the whole purpose of domain autonomy, or it gets quietly skipped. The fix — federated computational governance — is to keep the standards centrally defined but push enforcement into the platform itself: automated checks that a data product can't be published without a classification tag, an owner, and a passing quality check, enforced the same way for every domain without a human in the loop for routine cases. I'd tell that leader: the policies might look similar on paper, but if we don't rebuild how they're enforced, mesh governance either doesn't scale or doesn't happen.
commonMistakes: Assumes governance mechanics stay the same when only data location changes
Doesn't explain what 'federated computational governance' specifically means (automated, platform-enforced policy at publish time)
Fails to explain why domain ownership removes the single point of enforcement a central warehouse relied on
Describes mesh governance as 'no governance' or 'full central control,' missing the actual federated middle ground
keyPoints: Explains how centralized governance's enforcement mechanism depends on the governance team also controlling the pipeline
Defines federated computational governance as centrally-defined, platform-automated enforcement at the point of publication
Explains why mesh ownership removes the old single point of control
Connects the mechanism change to real risk if enforcement isn't automated (governance decay to ad hoc domain decisions)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly contrasts centralized enforcement with federated computational governance
Explains why domain ownership forces a mechanism change, not just a location change
Identifies the risk of governance decay without automated enforcement

questions.title: Why a Single Metadata Repository Doesn't Scale Across a Multi-Platform Enterprise
questions.prompt: A well-meaning architect proposes manually copying every table's metadata into one master spreadsheet-turned-database so there's 'one place' to look things up. Explain why this passive, manually-maintained approach breaks down at enterprise scale, and what 'active metadata' means as the architectural alternative.
questions.modelAnswer: A manually-maintained single repository has two structural problems that get worse, not better, as the enterprise grows: it requires someone to notice every change in every source system and manually re-enter it, so it's perpetually stale the moment any schema, owner, or classification changes anywhere in the estate; and it has no mechanism to verify its own accuracy against the live systems it's describing, so staleness is invisible until someone relies on wrong metadata and gets burned. 'Active metadata' is the architectural answer: instead of metadata being a static description someone typed in once, it's continuously harvested and kept current through automated scanning and integration connectors that read the real state of source systems (schema, usage patterns, access patterns, query logs, lineage events) and update the catalog automatically, and — critically — that metadata is then used operationally to trigger actions, not just to be looked up: an active metadata platform can automatically flag a newly-created table with no classification, auto-suggest an owner based on who's actually querying it, or feed a policy engine that blocks access until classification is complete. The shift is from metadata as documentation (passive, manually curated, trusted on faith) to metadata as a live operational signal (automated, continuously verified against reality, acted upon by the platform itself) — which is the only way a catalog describing thousands of tables across many platforms stays trustworthy without an impossibly large manual-curation team.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk that architect through what happens six months after the spreadsheet-database goes live: half the tables it describes have already changed, nobody updated the description, and now people are making decisions off information that's quietly wrong — which is worse than having no catalog at all, because at least then people knew to go check the source. The fix isn't 'try harder to keep it updated manually,' it's a different architecture: active metadata, where the catalog is continuously refreshed by automated scanners and integrations that read the real state of each system, rather than by a human remembering to update a record. And the metadata doesn't just sit there to be looked up — it actively does something, like flagging an unclassified new table or feeding an access-policy engine. I'd frame it as: passive metadata is a snapshot that ages the moment you take it; active metadata is a live feed, and at enterprise scale, a live feed is the only version that stays honest.
commonMistakes: Doesn't identify staleness and lack of verification as the core failure of manual approaches
Treats 'add more process discipline' as a fix for a fundamentally manual, unscalable mechanism
Can't define active metadata beyond 'automated scanning' — misses the operational/action-triggering aspect
Assumes a single central repository is inherently the right target architecture regardless of mechanism

Defines active metadata as continuously harvested and operationally actionable, not just automatically scanned
Gives a concrete example of active metadata triggering an action (auto-flagging, auto-suggesting an owner)
Frames the shift as documentation versus live operational signal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why passive, manual metadata maintenance fails at scale

questions.title: Classifications vs. Sensitivity Labels in Purview: Different Jobs
questions.prompt: A new governance analyst asks why Purview has both 'classifications' and 'sensitivity labels' when they both seem to be about tagging sensitive data. Explain the distinct job each one does, how they interact, and why skipping either one leaves a real gap.
questions.modelAnswer: A classification in Purview answers the descriptive question: what kind of data is this, factually — a credit card number, a US Social Security Number, an email address — detected automatically by scanning content against system or custom pattern-matching rules, and attached to the specific column or asset where that data type was found. A sensitivity label answers a different, prescriptive question: given what this data is, how should it be handled — can it be shared externally, does it need encryption, should it trigger a watermark or access restriction in Microsoft 365 — and labels carry enforceable protection actions (via Microsoft Purview Information Protection) rather than just describing content. The two interact in a specific direction: classification results can inform and even auto-apply a sensitivity label (a column classified as containing SSNs can trigger an auto-labeling rule that applies a 'Highly Confidential' label), but a label itself doesn't scan or detect anything — it's the policy consequence that rides on top of a classification finding. Skipping classification and only using labels means labels get applied manually and inconsistently, missing sensitive data nobody thought to label. Skipping labels and only using classification means you know exactly what's sensitive but have no enforced handling policy attached to it — you've diagnosed the problem without doing anything about it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as description versus consequence. Classification is Purview automatically figuring out and tagging what a piece of data actually is — this column has SSNs in it — based on scanning content. A sensitivity label is the handling rule that gets attached once you know that: this data needs to be encrypted, or can't leave the tenant, or gets a watermark. The useful thing is that classification findings can drive automatic labeling, so you're not relying on someone to notice and manually apply the right label every time. If you only do classification, you'll know where your sensitive data is but nothing is actually protecting it differently because of that knowledge. If you only do labeling without classification feeding it, you're relying on people to manually apply the right label, which doesn't scale and misses things. I'd tell the analyst: classification finds it, labeling protects it, and the real governance value is in wiring the first into the second automatically.
commonMistakes: Treats classification and sensitivity labels as interchangeable or redundant
Doesn't explain that labels carry enforceable protection actions, unlike classifications
Misses that classification findings can drive auto-labeling rules
Can't articulate the concrete gap left by using only one mechanism
keyPoints: Correctly defines classification as automated content-based detection of data type
Correctly defines sensitivity labels as the enforceable handling/protection policy
Explains the auto-labeling interaction between classification and labels
Explains the concrete gap left by skipping either mechanism

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes classification from sensitivity labels
Explains how classification findings can drive automatic labeling
Explains the concrete gap from skipping either mechanism
Communicates clearly to a junior analyst

questions.title: Unity Catalog's Three-Level Namespace and Metastore Scope at Enterprise Scale
questions.prompt: An enterprise architect proposes a single Unity Catalog metastore for a global company's entire Databricks footprint across every region, to 'keep it simple.' Explain the three-level namespace (catalog.schema.table) and why metastore scope specifically — not just catalog or schema design — is the decision that matters most at this scale.
questions.modelAnswer: Unity Catalog organizes data in a three-level namespace — catalog, then schema, then table — where the catalog is the top-level governance boundary (typically mapped to an environment or major business division), the schema groups related tables within it, and the table is the actual data object; permissions and most governance policy are defined and inherited down through this hierarchy. The reason metastore scope is the decision that matters most, more than how catalogs or schemas are organized within it, is that a metastore is a regional construct tied to a specific cloud region, and it's the actual boundary for where metadata and, depending on configuration, underlying storage can live — a single global metastore means every catalog, schema, and table's metadata is anchored to one region, which directly conflicts with data residency requirements that many jurisdictions impose (EU data must stay in the EU, for instance). Catalog and schema design can be fixed later with a reorganization; metastore placement effectively cannot be changed without a disruptive migration, because it's the physical/regional anchor everything else is built on top of. So the right enterprise answer is almost always metastore-per-region (or per major compliance boundary), with a consistent catalog/schema naming convention applied within each metastore so the experience feels unified even though the underlying metastores are regionally separated — 'simple' in this context has to mean 'consistent policy and naming,' not 'one physical metastore,' because the latter creates a residency problem that's expensive to unwind.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop that proposal before it goes further, because metastore scope is the one decision in this hierarchy that's genuinely hard to undo. The three-level namespace — catalog, schema, table — is how Unity Catalog organizes everything, and catalogs and schemas can be reorganized later if we get the structure wrong. A metastore is different: it's tied to a region, and it's the actual anchor for where this data's metadata lives, which matters enormously the moment you have any data residency requirement — and most global companies have at least one. One global metastore means we've effectively decided every region's data lives under one region's metastore, which is a compliance problem waiting to surface, not a simplicity win. My recommendation is metastore-per-region, with the 'simple' part coming from a shared naming convention and governance policy applied consistently across each one, not from collapsing them into a single physical metastore.
commonMistakes: Treats metastore scope as equivalent in flexibility to catalog or schema design
Proposes a single global metastore without considering data residency implications
Confuses the three-level namespace ordering (catalog.schema.table)
Doesn't distinguish 'simple to use' (consistent naming/policy) from 'simple architecture' (one physical metastore)
keyPoints: Correctly explains the catalog.schema.table three-level namespace and its governance role
Explains that a metastore is a regional construct and the hardest layer to change later
Connects metastore scope directly to data residency compliance requirements
Recommends metastore-per-region with consistent naming/policy as the practical enterprise pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the three-level namespace
Correctly identifies metastore scope as region-bound and hard to change
Connects metastore scope to data residency requirements
Recommends a sound enterprise pattern (metastore-per-region)

questions.title: Why Snowflake's Role Hierarchy Breaks Down Without a Naming Convention at Scale
questions.prompt: A Snowflake account has grown organically to over 300 roles with names like 'ANALYST2,' 'TEMP_ACCESS,' and 'REPORTING_V2_FIXED,' and nobody is confident anymore about what any given role actually grants. Explain how Snowflake's role hierarchy is supposed to work, the functional-role versus access-role distinction, and why this specific failure mode happens at scale.
questions.modelAnswer: Snowflake's RBAC model is a hierarchy where roles can be granted to other roles, forming an inheritance chain, and a user is granted one or more roles directly, inheriting every privilege of every role beneath it in that chain. The scalable pattern separates two layers: access roles, which map directly to a specific privilege on a specific object or object type (e.g., SELECT on the SALES schema), and functional roles, which represent a business function or job (e.g., SALES_ANALYST) and are composed by granting the relevant access roles to them — so a functional role is a bundle of access roles, and a user gets a functional role rather than being granted a pile of individual access roles directly. The failure in this scenario happens because that separation was never enforced: roles were created ad hoc whenever someone needed access, named for convenience at the time rather than for what they actually grant, and access roles and functional roles got blended together with no naming convention distinguishing them — so 'ANALYST2' could be a functional role, an access role, or a one-off grant nobody remembers creating. At 300+ roles with no systematic structure, the hierarchy technically still works mechanically, but it's become unauditable, because you can no longer answer 'what can this role actually do' without manually tracing its full grant chain every single time. The fix is a naming convention that encodes the access/functional distinction and the object/privilege it maps to, plus an audit to collapse or retire undocumented roles.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the intended model first: access roles tied to one specific privilege on one specific thing, functional roles that bundle those access roles into something that maps to an actual job, and users get functional roles, not a grab-bag of access roles. What went wrong here is that distinction was never enforced — people created roles whenever they needed something, named them for whatever made sense that day, and now 'TEMP_ACCESS' could grant anything and nobody remembers what. The hierarchy itself isn't broken mechanically, Snowflake is still inheriting grants correctly — the problem is nobody can audit it anymore because the naming and structure don't tell you anything. My fix is a naming convention that makes the access/functional split visible in the name itself, an audit pass that traces every one of those 300 roles back to its actual grants, and a retirement plan for anything that's clearly dead weight or duplicated. I wouldn't try to rename everything overnight — I'd stop new ad hoc role creation first, then work through the backlog.

Blames the role hierarchy mechanism itself rather than the lack of naming/structural discipline
Proposes a full rename/restructure without first stopping new ad hoc role creation
Treats this as a one-time cleanup rather than a governance process gap that will recur without a convention

Explains the access-role vs. functional-role separation pattern
Diagnoses the failure as a missing naming convention/structural discipline, not a mechanism flaw
Proposes both an audit/cleanup and a forward-looking convention to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Promoted vs. Certified: Why Power BI's Endorsement Levels Aren't Just Badges
questions.prompt: A business user asks why it matters whether a Power BI dataset is 'promoted' or 'certified' — both show a badge, so what's actually different? Explain the organizational meaning of each endorsement level, who should be able to grant each one, and why treating them as interchangeable undermines trust in the semantic layer.
questions.modelAnswer: Promoted and Certified are deliberately different levels of organizational trust, not cosmetic variants of the same badge. Promotion is self-asserted and low-barrier: a content owner marks their own report or dataset as promoted to signal 'I believe this is good, reusable work,' and in most tenant configurations any content owner can promote their own content without a review step — it's useful for surfacing quality work but carries no independent verification. Certification is meant to be the opposite: it signals that content has been reviewed and approved by a designated authority (typically a central BI or governance team, restricted via tenant settings to specific security groups) against defined quality, accuracy, and ownership-maintenance standards, and because that authority is restricted, a certified badge should mean something consistent across the entire tenant rather than varying by who happened to click the button. If promotion and certification are treated as interchangeable — especially if certification permissions aren't actually restricted — the certified badge stops being a trust signal at all, because business users build reports on top of a 'certified' dataset assuming it passed a real review, when in practice some certified datasets passed a review and others were self-certified by an enthusiastic owner. That erosion is exactly how organizations end up with the 'two certified datasets disagree' problem — certification only functions as intended when the organization is disciplined about who can grant it and what passing that bar actually requires.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it to that user in terms of who's vouching for the content. Promoted means the person who built it is vouching for their own work — useful, but it's self-reported, and anyone with ownership can do it. Certified is supposed to mean someone independent, usually a central governance or BI team, actually reviewed it against real standards before that badge went on. The reason I care about keeping those separate is trust: the whole point of a certified badge is that people downstream don't have to re-verify the data themselves, they can trust the badge. If we let certification permissions sprawl so that anyone can self-certify, or if we treat promoted and certified as basically the same thing, that trust signal is gone, and we're right back to people quietly re-validating every number because they don't actually know what 'certified' means anymore in this tenant. I'd push to lock certification down to a specific governance group and make the bar for it explicit and documented.
commonMistakes: Treats promoted and certified as functionally equivalent badges
Doesn't know certification permissions should be restricted via tenant settings to a specific group
Misses the self-asserted (promoted) versus independently-reviewed (certified) distinction
Doesn't connect endorsement discipline to the broader 'which number do I trust' governance problem
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes self-asserted promotion from independently-reviewed certification
Explains that certification permission should be tenant-restricted to a governance authority
Connects endorsement discipline to overall trust in the semantic layer
Explains what erodes when certification isn't actually gatekept

questions.title: Where Cloud Provider Responsibility Ends and Governance Responsibility Begins
questions.prompt: A stakeholder assumes that because your data lake sits in Azure/AWS, the cloud provider is handling 'security and compliance' for it. Explain the shared responsibility model specifically as it applies to data governance — what the provider actually secures, and what remains the organization's job regardless of which cloud it's in.
questions.modelAnswer: The shared responsibility model draws a line at the infrastructure boundary: the cloud provider is responsible for the security and availability of the underlying physical infrastructure, the virtualization layer, and the managed service itself (patching the storage service, physically securing the data center, guaranteeing the durability SLA) — but everything about what data lives in that infrastructure, who can access it, and how it's classified and governed is the customer's responsibility, in both Azure and AWS, regardless of which specific services are used. Concretely, for data governance that means: the provider does not decide or enforce your data classification scheme, does not know which columns contain PII versus public data, does not configure your access control policies or review who has standing access to a storage account or bucket, does not define your retention policy, and does not monitor for governance-relevant anomalies like a service principal suddenly reading far more data than its normal pattern — all of that is the organization's responsibility to design, implement, and operate using the provider's tools (IAM, encryption key management, policy engines, logging) as building blocks, not as something that comes pre-configured correctly. The provider secures the building; the organization is still fully responsible for deciding who gets which keys and classifying what's inside each room, and a surprising number of real breaches and compliance failures trace back to an organization assuming the provider's infrastructure security covered a governance decision it never actually made.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct that assumption directly, because it's one of the more common and more dangerous misunderstandings I run into. The cloud provider secures the infrastructure underneath everything — the physical data centers, the hypervisor, the durability of the storage service — and that's genuinely strong and something we don't need to re-litigate. But the provider has no idea what's actually inside our storage account or S3 bucket, doesn't know which columns are PII, didn't configure our access policies, and isn't monitoring for governance-specific red flags like a service account suddenly pulling far more data than usual. All of that is on us, using the provider's tools — IAM, encryption, policy engines — as the raw materials, not as something that arrives pre-built correctly. I'd tell that stakeholder: think of it as the provider securing the building and the locks on the doors, but we're still the ones deciding who gets a key to which room and what's stored in each one.

Doesn't draw the line at the infrastructure/managed-service boundary correctly
Treats the shared responsibility model as cloud-specific rather than consistent across Azure and AWS
Can't give a concrete example of a governance responsibility that remains with the organization

questions.title: Does AI Governance Replace Data Governance, or Extend It?
questions.prompt: A newly-formed AI governance committee wants to stand up entirely separate stewardship roles, a separate catalog, and a separate glossary from the existing data governance program, arguing that AI is fundamentally different. Explain whether that's the right structural call, and what AI governance should actually build on top of versus duplicate.
questions.modelAnswer: AI governance is best understood as an extension of an existing data governance program, not a parallel one, because the underlying assets a model is governed around — the training data, the features, the data owners who understand what that data actually means — are the same assets the existing program already catalogs, classifies, and assigns stewards to; duplicating that structure means maintaining two conflicting records of 'who owns this data' and two glossaries that will inevitably drift apart and define the same term differently. What genuinely is new and does warrant distinct additions are the AI-specific layers that sit on top of the existing foundation: a model inventory/registry (which doesn't exist in a pure data governance program), model documentation standards (model cards), AI-specific lineage connecting training snapshots to model versions to predictions, and a review/approval process for models before production deployment — none of which a traditional data governance program covers, but all of which should reference the same business glossary, the same data classification taxonomy, and ideally the same stewards already accountable for the data a model consumes. The right structural call is: extend the existing catalog and glossary with AI-specific asset types and metadata fields, add new roles (a model owner, a model risk reviewer) that work alongside existing data stewards rather than replacing them, and resist the urge to stand up parallel infrastructure just because the use case feels different — the risk types are genuinely new, but the governed objects underneath (data) mostly aren't.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on building that in parallel, because I've seen what happens when two glossaries exist for the same organization — they drift, and eventually someone's model documentation says 'active customer' means one thing while the data governance program's glossary says something else, and now you have the exact conflicting-numbers problem governance exists to prevent, just one layer up. My recommendation is to extend what already exists: the same catalog, the same glossary, the same classification taxonomy, with new asset types layered on for models, and new roles — model owner, model risk reviewer — that sit alongside the data stewards who already understand that data, not instead of them. What's genuinely new in AI governance is the model inventory, model documentation standards, and the approval workflow before a model ships — none of that existed before, and it deserves real new structure. But the foundational question of 'what is this data, who owns it, what does this term mean' shouldn't get a second, competing answer just because a model is now involved.
commonMistakes: Proposes a fully parallel AI governance structure instead of extending the existing program
Doesn't identify the real risk of two glossaries/catalogs drifting into disagreement
Fails to name what genuinely is new in AI governance (model inventory, model cards, approval workflow)
Treats 'AI is different' as justification for duplicating infrastructure rather than adding to it

Identifies the risk of catalog/glossary drift from parallel structures
Correctly names the genuinely new AI-specific additions (model registry, model cards, AI lineage, approval workflow)
Proposes new roles that complement, rather than replace, existing data stewards

Correctly names the genuinely new AI-specific governance additions

questions.title: Fix a Non-SARGable, Non-Covering Query Under Load
questions.prompt:
You're handed this production query that's doing a full clustered index scan on a 40-million-row table, confirmed via SET STATISTICS IO showing logical reads in the hundreds of thousands:

SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) = '06/15/2013'
   AND UPPER(Status) = 'SHIPPED';

Rewrite the query to be SARGable, and write the covering index you'd create to support it, explaining your column order choice.
questions.modelAnswer: There are two non-SARGable predicates here, and both need fixing. CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) wraps the date column in a function, forcing a scan even if an index exists; UPPER(Status) does the same to the status column. The date predicate should be rewritten as a half-open range against the raw column; the status predicate should compare against the literal in its natural case, relying on the column's collation to be case-insensitive rather than forcing a transformation on every row. For the covering index, the equality predicate (Status) should lead the key, since equality columns belong before range columns in a composite index — this lets SQL Server seek to the exact Status value, then scan only the OrderDate range within that narrower slice — and the remaining selected columns go into INCLUDE so the plan never needs a Key Lookup back to the clustered index.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out there are actually two separate problems stacked in that one WHERE clause, not one. The CONVERT around OrderDate and the UPPER around Status are both doing the same damage — wrapping the column so the index can't be used no matter how well it's built. I'd rewrite the date as a range against the raw column and drop the UPPER, trusting the collation to handle case. Then for the index, I always put the equality column first — Status — because that lets SQL Server narrow down to an exact value before it even has to think about the date range, and I'd include the rest of the selected columns so we get a fully covering seek with no extra trip back to the clustered index.
questions.example:
-- SARGable rewrite
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE Status = 'Shipped'
  AND OrderDate >= '2013-06-15' AND OrderDate < '2013-06-16';

-- Covering index: equality column first, then the range column, then INCLUDE the rest
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_SalesOrderHeader_Status_OrderDate
ON Sales.SalesOrderHeader (Status, OrderDate)
INCLUDE (OrderID, CustomerID, TotalDue);
commonMistakes: Only fixes one of the two non-SARGable predicates
Puts the range column before the equality column in the index key
Forgets INCLUDE columns, leaving a Key Lookup in the plan
Assumes UPPER() is needed without checking the column's collation

questions.title: Find the Head of a Live Blocking Chain
questions.prompt: Users are reporting the application is frozen. You suspect blocking, not an outage. Write the T-SQL you'd run right now against the live server to find the head blocker — the session that isn't waiting on anyone else but is blocking everyone downstream — and explain what you'd do with the session ID once you have it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests joined to sys.dm_exec_sessions, filtering for sessions that have a non-zero blocking_session_id to see everyone currently blocked, then specifically look for the blocking_session_id value that does not itself appear as a session_id with its own non-zero blocking_session_id — that session is the head blocker, the one actually holding the lock everyone else is waiting on. Once I have it, I'd pull its current or last statement via sys.dm_exec_sql_text and check open_tran_count and last_request_start_time to understand what it's actually doing and how long it's been doing it, rather than acting blind. Only if it's clearly stuck or abnormally long-running would I consider KILLing the session, understanding that the kill itself rolls back its transaction and can take as long or longer than letting it finish. The real fix afterward is to find out why that session held locks so long — a missing index causing a slow scan while holding a write lock, or application code that doesn't commit promptly — because KILL is an emergency release valve, not a repeatable procedure.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'the app is frozen,' my first move is never to panic and start killing sessions — it's to find out if this is actually blocking, and if so, where it starts. I'd run a query against dm_exec_requests joined to dm_exec_sessions, filtering for anyone currently blocked, and then specifically look for the one session that's blocking others but isn't itself waiting on anyone — that's my head blocker. Before I touch it, I want to know what it's actually running and how long it's been running it, because killing it rolls back its transaction, and that rollback can take just as long as letting it finish. Once things are stable again, the real work starts: finding out why that session held locks that long in the first place, because if I don't fix that, I'm back here again next week.
questions.example:
SELECT 
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    t.text AS running_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.session_id IN (
    SELECT blocking_session_id FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0
)
AND r.blocking_session_id = 0;  -- the head blocker: blocking others, blocked by no one

Confuses a long-running query with a blocking chain — not every slow query is blocking others
Doesn't capture what the head blocker's own transaction was doing before acting

Explains the difference between being blocked and being the source of blocking
