questions.title: Fix a Skewed 40-Million-Row Join With Key Salting
questions.prompt: The join from the earlier skew diagnosis (40M-row transactions table joining a dimension table on customer_id, with one customer_id responsible for roughly 60% of all rows) needs an actual code fix, not just a diagnosis. Write the PySpark code to salt the skewed key and produce a correct, balanced join.
questions.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

SALT_BUCKETS = 20
skewed_keys = ["CUST_00000"]  # known hot key(s) from prior diagnosis

# Split the fact table: skewed rows get a random salt, normal rows get salt = 0
txns_salted = transactions.withColumn(
    "salt",
    F.when(F.col("customer_id").isin(skewed_keys), (F.rand() * SALT_BUCKETS).cast("int"))
     .otherwise(F.lit(0))
)

# Explode the dimension table: one row per salt bucket for the skewed keys, one row (salt=0) for everyone else
dim_exploded = dim_customer.withColumn(
    "salt",
    F.explode(
        F.when(F.col("customer_id").isin(skewed_keys), F.array([F.lit(i) for i in range(SALT_BUCKETS)]))
         .otherwise(F.array(F.lit(0)))
    )
)

joined = txns_salted.join(
    dim_exploded,
    on=["customer_id", "salt"],
    how="inner"
).drop("salt")
questions.modelAnswer: Salting breaks up the one oversized shuffle partition created by hash-partitioning on a skewed key, by artificially sub-dividing that key into SALT_BUCKETS synthetic sub-keys so the shuffle spreads its rows across many partitions instead of one. The fact table gets a random salt column, but only for rows carrying a known skewed key -- everyone else gets salt=0 and is otherwise untouched. The dimension table must be exploded so it has a matching row for every salt bucket the skewed key could have produced; without this, the join on (customer_id, salt) would only match salt=0 dimension rows and silently drop the skewed-key fact rows entirely, turning a performance fix into a correctness bug. The result is the same logical join -- the skewed key's rows are now parallelized across SALT_BUCKETS tasks, and the non-skewed 99%+ of the data produces an identical result to the unsalted join since both sides use salt=0. The cost is a small duplication of dimension rows for the skewed key only, negligible if the dimension table is small. This is the manual version of what AQE's skew join optimization now does automatically in most cases -- worth trying spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled first, reaching for manual salting only when AQE doesn't detect or handle this specific pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: The part people usually get wrong the first time they try this is forgetting to explode the dimension side. If you only salt the fact table and join on (customer_id, salt) against an unmodified dimension table, every row you just salted to anything other than 0 silently fails to match and disappears from the output -- you've fixed the skew and broken the join at the same time, and it's easy not to notice because the job runs fast now, which looks like success. So I always build this in two matched halves: salt the hot key on the fact side, then make sure the dimension side has one row per possible salt value for that same key before I even run it. I'd also check AQE's skew join setting first, since a lot of what used to require this by hand is now handled automatically, and I'd rather not maintain custom salting logic if I don't have to.
commonMistakes: Salts the fact table but forgets to explode the dimension table, causing skewed-key rows to silently drop out of the join
Salts every row uniformly instead of only the known skewed key(s), unnecessarily inflating the join for normal data
Doesn't verify AQE's automatic skew join handling first before reaching for manual salting
Uses a salt bucket count too small to actually spread the hot key across enough partitions
Forgets to drop the salt column after the join, leaking an implementation detail into downstream schema
keyPoints: Salts only the known skewed key(s) on the fact side, leaving the rest of the data untouched
Explodes the dimension table to produce a matching row per salt bucket for the skewed key
Joins on the composite (customer_id, salt) key to preserve correctness
Recognizes this as the manual equivalent of AQE's automatic skew join handling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct salting logic applied selectively to the skewed key
Correctly explodes the dimension side to avoid dropping matched rows
Produces a correct, logically equivalent join result
Notes the AQE skew-join alternative/relationship

questions.title: Writing a Custom Classification Rule for a Non-Standard ID Format
questions.prompt: Your company issues internal "Employee Badge IDs" in the format EMP-NNNNNN-XX (six digits, then a two-letter site code), and no Purview system classification covers this pattern. Define the custom classification rule (regex pattern and minimum data-match requirements) you'd register in Purview, and explain how you'd validate it before enabling it tenant-wide.
questions.modelAnswer: A custom classification in Purview needs both a content pattern and sensible thresholds, because a regex alone will produce false positives on any column that happens to contain similarly-shaped strings. The regex ^EMP-\d{6}-[A-Z]{2}$ anchors on the full value so it won't match a substring inside a longer free-text field. I'd also add a column-name pattern as a secondary signal (matching 'badge' or variations of 'employee id') so the classifier weights columns whose name suggests the right content more heavily, reducing false positives from coincidentally-shaped data elsewhere. The minimumPercentageMatch and minimumMatchCount thresholds matter because they control how much of a sampled column has to match before Purview actually applies the classification — too low, and a column with a handful of incidental matches gets mislabeled; too high, and a genuinely-populated but sparsely-filled badge ID column gets missed. Before enabling tenant-wide, I'd run it against a small, known set of registered sources first (a test scan on sources I already know contain real badge IDs, and at least one source I know doesn't), check the scan results for false positives and false negatives, and only then add it to the production scan rule set — rolling a new custom classification out untested across every source risks mislabeling data at scale on the first run.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just write the regex and ship it — the regex is maybe a third of the actual rule. I'd anchor the pattern to the full value so it doesn't partially match something unrelated, and I'd pair it with a column-name hint, because content-only matching on a format this generic-looking (digits and letters) is going to produce false positives somewhere in a large estate. Then I'd actually tune the match thresholds instead of leaving them at defaults, because that's what decides whether a sparsely-populated real column gets classified or a coincidentally-shaped column gets mislabeled. Before I let this run tenant-wide, I test it against sources I already know the answer for — one with real badge IDs, one without — and I look at the actual scan output, not just 'did it run successfully.' A custom classification that's wrong doesn't fail loudly, it just quietly mislabels things, so validation before rollout isn't optional here.
commonMistakes: Writes an unanchored regex that partial-matches unrelated content
Skips the column-name hint, relying on content pattern alone and increasing false positives
Leaves match-percentage/match-count thresholds at defaults without considering the tradeoff
Enables the new classification tenant-wide without first validating against known sources
keyPoints: Writes a correctly anchored regex matching the full expected format
Adds a column-name pattern as a secondary signal to reduce false positives
Explains the purpose of match-percentage/match-count thresholds
Describes a validation step against known sources before tenant-wide rollout

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, properly anchored regex pattern
Includes and justifies a column-name secondary signal
Correctly explains and sets match thresholds
Describes a sound pre-rollout validation approach

questions.title: Granting Scoped Access With Unity Catalog Row Filters and Column Masks
questions.prompt: Write the SQL to (1) create and apply a row filter so a sales analyst role only sees rows for their own region on the customers table, and (2) create and apply a column mask that redacts the SSN column for everyone except a compliance role.
questions.code:
-- Row filter function: restrict rows to the caller's own region
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION governance.region_row_filter(region STRING)
RETURN is_account_group_member('compliance_team')
    OR region = current_user_region();

ALTER TABLE sales.customers
SET ROW FILTER governance.region_row_filter ON (region);

-- Column mask function: redact SSN unless caller is in the compliance role
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION governance.mask_ssn(ssn STRING)
RETURN CASE
    WHEN is_account_group_member('compliance_team') THEN ssn
    ELSE 'XXX-XX-' || RIGHT(ssn, 4)
END;

ALTER TABLE sales.customers
ALTER COLUMN ssn SET MASK governance.mask_ssn;
questions.modelAnswer: Row filters and column masks in Unity Catalog are both implemented as SQL functions registered against the table, evaluated per query at runtime rather than by maintaining separate filtered views or physical copies of the data — this matters because it means the same underlying table serves every role correctly without duplicating storage or risking the views drifting out of sync with the base table. The row filter function takes the column being filtered as a parameter and returns a boolean; I'd write it to always allow the compliance team an exception (since compliance typically needs cross-region visibility for audits) and otherwise compare against a helper that resolves the current user's assigned region, rather than hardcoding region logic per role. The column mask function similarly takes the masked column's value and returns either the real value or a redacted form, branching on group membership via is_account_group_member — a built-in that checks Unity Catalog's identity federation rather than requiring a separate permissions table. A critical detail: both are applied via ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER / SET MASK, attaching the policy directly to the table rather than requiring every consumer to remember to query through a special view, so the protection travels with the table regardless of which tool or workspace queries it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd emphasize here is that both of these are attached directly to the table, not implemented as a separate 'secure view' that people have to remember to use instead of the real table — because the moment protection depends on remembering to use the right object, someone eventually queries the base table directly and bypasses it. So I write a row filter function that returns true for compliance (who need to see everything) or for rows matching the caller's own region, and I attach it straight to the customers table with ALTER TABLE SET ROW FILTER. Same pattern for the SSN mask — a function that returns the real value only for compliance, and a redacted form for everyone else, attached with SET MASK. Both checks use is_account_group_member so they're driven by actual group membership rather than a hand-maintained permissions table that can drift out of date.
commonMistakes: Implements filtering as a separate view instead of attaching a row filter/mask directly to the table
Hardcodes role names into per-row logic instead of using is_account_group_member or an equivalent group check
Forgets to give compliance (or another legitimate audit role) an explicit bypass in the filter logic
Masks the column by truncating or hashing in a way that breaks legitimate partial-match use cases without checking requirements first
keyPoints: Correctly writes a row filter function attached via ALTER TABLE SET ROW FILTER
Correctly writes a column mask function attached via ALTER TABLE ALTER COLUMN SET MASK
Uses group-membership checks (is_account_group_member) rather than hardcoded logic
Explains why attaching policy to the table itself is safer than a separate filtered view

Correct, working column mask SQL

questions.title: Building a Snowflake Masking Policy and Row Access Policy Together
questions.prompt: Write the SQL to create a masking policy that shows email addresses in full only to COMPLIANCE_ROLE (masked for everyone else), a row access policy restricting rows to a user's assigned region, and apply both to a CUSTOMERS table.
questions.modelAnswer: Both policies are schema-level objects in Snowflake, created independently of the table and then attached to it, which lets the same policy be reused across multiple tables that share the same column semantics instead of redefining masking logic per table. The masking policy is a named function keyed on CURRENT_ROLE(), branching to return the real value for the compliance role and a masked form (here, a regex that keeps the domain but obscures the local part) for everyone else — Snowflake evaluates this at query time, so the same underlying stored value serves both audiences without duplicating the column. The row access policy works the same way structurally, but returns a boolean per row rather than a transformed value — true means the row is visible to the current session, so I give compliance an unconditional pass and otherwise join against a maintained user-to-region mapping table rather than hardcoding usernames into the policy itself, since that mapping needs to be updatable without redefining the policy. The ALTER TABLE ... SET MASKING POLICY and ALTER TABLE ... ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY statements are what actually bind each policy to the real column/table; defining the policy alone does nothing until it's attached.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build these as two separate, reusable policy objects rather than one-off logic baked into a view, because the real win here is being able to attach the same masking policy to the email column on other tables later without rewriting it. The masking policy checks CURRENT_ROLE() and either returns the real email or a masked version — I keep the domain visible in the mask because that's often still useful for support teams without exposing the full address. For row access, I don't hardcode region logic into the policy itself — I join against a maintained mapping table of username to region, so when someone's region changes I update one row in that mapping table instead of redefining the policy. And I always give compliance an explicit bypass in both, because the last thing you want is your own audit team getting masked out of the data they're supposed to be reviewing. The two ALTER TABLE statements at the end are what actually turn these from defined objects into enforced policy — easy step to forget.
commonMistakes: Hardcodes usernames or regions directly into the policy instead of joining a maintainable mapping table
Forgets to actually bind the policy to the table/column via ALTER TABLE after creating it
Doesn't give compliance/audit roles an explicit bypass, locking out the team that needs full visibility
Masks the email so completely that support/legitimate partial-match use cases break unnecessarily
keyPoints: Correctly creates a masking policy keyed on CURRENT_ROLE()
Correctly creates a row access policy returning a boolean per row
Uses a maintainable mapping table rather than hardcoded values for region logic
Correctly binds both policies to the table via ALTER TABLE

Correct, working row access policy SQL
Uses a maintainable approach to role/region logic
Correctly binds both policies to the table

questions.title: Writing Row-Level Security DAX for a Manager-Based Hierarchy
questions.prompt: Write the Power BI row-level security DAX role expression that restricts an employee data table so each manager sees their direct and indirect reports, using an Employees table with EmployeeID and ManagerID columns and PATH-style hierarchy functions.
questions.modelAnswer: The hierarchy has to be materialized before RLS can filter against it, because DAX row-level security roles can only apply static filter predicates to the model as it loads — they can't recursively walk a self-referencing ManagerID relationship at query time. The PATH function builds that materialization: it concatenates each employee's ancestor chain (EmployeeID through ManagerID up to the root) into a delimited string column, computed once as part of the model. The RLS expression then uses PATHCONTAINS to check whether the current viewer's own EmployeeID appears anywhere in a given row's ancestor path — which is true for the viewer's own row and every descendant's row, since a descendant's path includes every manager above them, including the viewer. LOOKUPVALUE resolves USERPRINCIPALNAME() (the Power BI Service's authenticated viewer identity) to that viewer's EmployeeID via a matching Email column, so the filter is driven by who's actually viewing the report, not a hardcoded value. This correctly handles indirect reports at any depth, which a simple ManagerID = viewer's ID filter would miss entirely — that would only show direct reports, one level deep.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key realization here is that RLS can't recursively traverse a manager hierarchy on its own — DAX roles apply a filter, they don't walk a tree at query time. So I materialize the tree first: a calculated PATH column that turns each employee's manager chain into one string I can search. Then the actual RLS filter is just PATHCONTAINS checking whether the viewer's own ID shows up anywhere in that row's ancestor path — which covers direct reports and reports-of-reports at any depth, because a deep report's path includes every manager above them. I resolve who the viewer is with USERPRINCIPALNAME matched against an Email column, so it's driven by the real logged-in user, not something I have to hardcode per report. I'd flag to the team that if they'd written ManagerID = viewer's ID instead, they'd only be filtering to direct reports, which is a subtle and easy mistake to ship.
commonMistakes: Filters only on ManagerID = viewer's ID, missing indirect reports beyond one level
Tries to implement recursive hierarchy logic directly in the RLS filter instead of materializing a PATH column first
Forgets to resolve USERPRINCIPALNAME() to the model's actual EmployeeID via a lookup
Doesn't account for the viewer seeing their own row (PATHCONTAINS naturally includes it, but candidates often miss explaining this)
keyPoints: Correctly materializes the hierarchy with a PATH calculated column
Correctly uses PATHCONTAINS in the RLS filter expression
Resolves the viewer's identity via USERPRINCIPALNAME() and a LOOKUPVALUE join
Explains why this correctly covers indirect reports at any depth

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct PATH calculated column
Correct PATHCONTAINS-based RLS filter expression
Correctly resolves viewer identity via USERPRINCIPALNAME
Explains why this handles indirect reports correctly

questions.title: Writing an Azure Policy to Enforce a Required Data Classification Tag
questions.prompt: Write the Azure Policy definition (JSON) that denies the creation of a storage account unless it carries a 'DataClassification' tag set to one of an approved list of values, and explain why Deny is the right effect here rather than Audit.
questions.modelAnswer: The policy rule needs two conditions combined with anyOf, because 'no tag' and 'wrong tag value' are both non-compliant states and a candidate who checks only for the tag's existence will let an invalid value like 'classification-tbd' slip through. The first branch checks tags['DataClassification'] exists: false to catch resources with no tag at all; the second uses a negated 'in' check against the approved value list to catch resources that have the tag but with a value outside the approved set — combining them with anyOf means either condition alone is enough to trigger denial. Deny is the right effect here, not Audit, because Audit only flags non-compliant resources after they're created, leaving a live storage account with unclassified or misclassified data sitting in the environment until someone reviews a compliance report and remediates it — for data classification specifically, that gap between creation and remediation is exactly the window where ungoverned data exposure happens. Audit is appropriate for policies where you're still building confidence in a rule's accuracy before blocking deployments on it; Deny is appropriate once the policy is validated and the actual goal is to prevent the ungoverned state from ever existing. I'd typically start a new policy in Audit mode against a test scope to catch false positives, then flip it to Deny once the team trusts it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this with two failure conditions, not one, because I've seen policies that only check tag existence get satisfied by someone tagging DataClassification as literally anything, including garbage values, which defeats the point. So the policy denies if the tag is missing OR if it's present but not one of the approved values. On Deny versus Audit: Audit just tells you after the fact that something's non-compliant, which means for a window of time — sometimes a long one — there's live infrastructure holding data with no real classification on it, and that's precisely the risk this policy exists to prevent. I'd use Deny once I trust the rule, but I'd be honest that I wouldn't flip straight to Deny on day one — I'd run it in Audit against a test scope first to make sure it's not going to block legitimate deployments on some edge case I didn't anticipate, and only promote it to Deny once I've seen clean results.

Scopes the policy to the wrong resource type or an overly broad 'mode' setting

Correctly chooses Deny as the effect, with justification
Explains the real risk of the Audit-only exposure window

questions.title: Granting Column-Level Access in AWS Lake Formation
questions.prompt: Write the AWS Lake Formation commands (CLI or equivalent) to grant a data-scientist IAM role SELECT access to a Glue table, excluding specific PII columns, and explain why this requires Lake Formation rather than a plain IAM/S3 policy.
questions.modelAnswer: A plain IAM or S3 bucket policy can only grant or deny access at the object/prefix level — it has no concept of a 'table' or a 'column,' because S3 just sees files. Lake Formation sits above S3 and the Glue Data Catalog specifically to add table- and column-level governance semantics that the storage layer itself doesn't have, which is exactly what this requirement needs: granting access to a table while excluding specific columns. The grant-permissions call targets a TableWithColumns resource with a ColumnWildcard and ExcludedColumnNames, which grants SELECT on every column of the table except the ones explicitly listed — this is the column-exclusion pattern, as opposed to an explicit inclusion list, and it's the right choice here because it automatically continues to exclude the named PII columns even if new columns are added to the table later, whereas an inclusion list would need to be updated every time a new non-PII column is added. Under the hood, Lake Formation enforces this by handing out temporary, scoped credentials when the principal queries through an integrated service (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR), rather than the principal having direct unmediated access to the underlying S3 objects — which is why Lake Formation permissions, not S3 bucket policy, are the actual control plane for this kind of fine-grained access.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain first why IAM and S3 policies can't do this at all: they only understand objects and prefixes, not tables or columns, so there's no way to say 'this role can query this table but not these three columns' at that layer. Lake Formation exists specifically to add that missing semantic layer on top of Glue's catalog. The grant itself uses a column wildcard with an exclusion list rather than naming every column I do want to include, and that's a deliberate choice — if someone adds a new, non-sensitive column to this table next quarter, my exclusion-based grant keeps working correctly without me having to remember to update it, whereas an inclusion list would silently need maintenance every time the schema changes. I'd also mention that this only works because the data scientist is expected to query through an integrated engine like Athena — Lake Formation hands out scoped temporary credentials at query time rather than this being enforced by the data scientist's role having direct S3 access.

Uses an inclusion list of allowed columns instead of an exclusion list, creating future maintenance risk
Doesn't explain that enforcement depends on querying through an integrated engine (Athena, Redshift Spectrum), not direct S3 access
Forgets that Lake Formation permissions require the underlying table to already be registered in the Glue Data Catalog and Lake Formation
keyPoints: Correctly explains why column-level grants require Lake Formation, not IAM/S3 policy alone
Writes a correct grant-permissions call using column exclusion
Justifies exclusion-list over inclusion-list for future-proofing
Explains the temporary-credential enforcement mechanism via integrated query engines

questions.title: Securing a OneLake Shortcut Across Domains
questions.prompt: The Sales domain needs a shortcut into the Finance domain's lakehouse, but only to one specific table (FactRevenue), without gaining broader access to anything else in Finance's lakehouse. Describe the concrete steps and permission grants you'd use in Microsoft Fabric to set this up correctly, and the mistake that would accidentally over-grant access.
questions.modelAnswer: A OneLake shortcut is a reference, not a copy — it makes the target location appear inside the consuming workspace's lakehouse, but data access is still governed by the permissions on the underlying source, not by the shortcut itself; creating the shortcut doesn't grant any new access by itself, it just creates the pointer. So the actual security work happens in two places: first, Finance's lakehouse needs a granular permission grant — using Fabric's data access roles (OneLake data access roles), I'd create a role scoped specifically to the FactRevenue table/folder path, not to the lakehouse root, and assign the Sales domain's security group to that role rather than to a broader lakehouse-level role. Second, the shortcut itself in the Sales workspace should be created pointing at that specific table path, not at the lakehouse root, so the pointer itself doesn't expose a wider surface even if permissions were ever loosened later. The mistake that over-grants access is creating the shortcut at the lakehouse root level and/or assigning Sales to a role that grants access to the whole lakehouse rather than a path-scoped role — in that case, the moment Finance adds a new sensitive table anywhere in that lakehouse, Sales inherits visibility into it automatically through the existing shortcut and role, with nobody having deliberately decided to grant that.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd make sure the team understands up front is that a shortcut doesn't grant access by itself — it's just a pointer, and the real permission has to be set on the source side. So in Finance's lakehouse, I'd create a OneLake data access role scoped to just the FactRevenue path, not the lakehouse root, and put Sales's security group on that specific role. Then I'd point the shortcut itself at that same table path rather than the lakehouse root. The mistake I've seen teams make is doing this at the root level for convenience — one shortcut to the whole lakehouse, one broad role — because it's less setup work today. The problem is that convenience silently expands every time Finance adds a new table to that lakehouse, because Sales's access was never actually scoped to FactRevenue, it was scoped to 'everything in this lakehouse,' and nobody explicitly decided that.

Scopes the data access role or shortcut at the lakehouse root instead of the specific table path
Doesn't account for the access silently expanding when new tables are added to the source lakehouse
Grants a broad existing role instead of creating a new, narrowly-scoped role for this specific need

Describes creating a path-scoped OneLake data access role on the source lakehouse
Scopes both the role and the shortcut to the specific table, not the lakehouse root
Identifies the root-level over-grant mistake and its silent future-expansion risk

Describes correct path-scoped role creation and assignment

questions.title: Writing the SQL Behind a Stewardship Coverage KPI
questions.prompt: Write a SQL query against governance metadata tables (data_elements and stewardship_assignments) that computes, per business domain, the percentage of critical data elements that currently have an assigned, active data steward.
questions.code:
SELECT
    de.business_domain,
    COUNT(*) AS critical_elements,
    SUM(CASE WHEN sa.is_active = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS elements_with_active_steward,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN sa.is_active = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DECIMAL(5,2))
        / COUNT(*) * 100 AS pct_covered
FROM data_elements de
LEFT JOIN stewardship_assignments sa
    ON sa.data_element_id = de.data_element_id
    AND sa.is_active = 1
WHERE de.is_critical = 1
GROUP BY de.business_domain
ORDER BY pct_covered ASC;
questions.modelAnswer: The LEFT JOIN is deliberate, not incidental: a critical data element with no stewardship_assignments row at all is exactly the gap this KPI exists to surface, and an INNER JOIN would silently drop those unassigned elements out of the result entirely, making coverage look artificially better than it is — this is one of the most common correctness bugs in governance-metric queries. The is_active filter on the join condition (rather than in the WHERE clause) matters too: a data element with only an inactive or expired stewardship assignment should count as uncovered, and filtering is_active inside the ON clause preserves the LEFT JOIN's behavior of keeping the data_elements row with a NULL match, whereas filtering it in WHERE would convert the LEFT JOIN back into an effective INNER JOIN and drop unmatched rows again. Grouping by business_domain and ordering by pct_covered ascending surfaces the worst-covered domains first, which is the actionable framing for a governance KPI — leadership generally wants to know where to intervene, not just the aggregate number. I'd also flag that is_critical filtering has to happen on the data_elements side before the join, which it does here, so the denominator is 'critical elements in this domain,' not 'all elements.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that actually matters in this query is the LEFT JOIN plus where the is_active condition lives. If I used an INNER JOIN, every critical data element with zero stewardship assignment would just vanish from the result, and the coverage percentage would look better than reality — which is the opposite of what a KPI like this is supposed to catch. So LEFT JOIN, and I put the is_active filter in the ON clause specifically so an element with only an expired assignment still shows up as a row with no active match, rather than disappearing because I filtered it in the WHERE clause after the fact. I order by pct_covered ascending because the point of this report isn't the aggregate number, it's showing leadership exactly which domains need stewards assigned first.
commonMistakes: Uses an INNER JOIN, silently dropping unassigned critical elements from the denominator
Filters is_active in the WHERE clause instead of the ON clause, collapsing the LEFT JOIN back to an INNER JOIN
Forgets to filter is_critical, diluting the metric with non-critical elements
Doesn't order or surface the worst-covered domains in an actionable way
keyPoints: Correctly uses LEFT JOIN so unassigned critical elements are counted, not dropped
Correctly places the is_active condition in the ON clause to preserve LEFT JOIN semantics
Correctly filters to critical elements as the denominator
Surfaces results in an actionable, ordered way

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct LEFT JOIN usage preventing silent drop of unassigned elements
Correct placement of is_active filter preserving LEFT JOIN semantics
Correct critical-element filtering and grouping
Produces an actionable, correctly ordered result

questions.title: Automating a Model Approval Gate With Policy as Code
questions.prompt: Write a Python validation function that a CI/CD model-promotion pipeline calls before registering a model as "Production" in the model registry, blocking the promotion unless a model card, a bias evaluation result, and a named model owner are all present and valid.
questions.modelAnswer: A policy-as-code gate like this has to be a hard blocker embedded in the pipeline itself, not a checklist a human is trusted to remember, because the whole point is that a model can't reach a 'Production' registry state unless the function returns allowed — there's no path around it. I check three governance artifacts explicitly: a model card with at minimum its intended_use populated (an empty or missing model card object is a common failure mode worth checking for, not just its presence); a bias evaluation that both passed and isn't stale, since a bias evaluation run eight months ago against an earlier version of the model doesn't actually tell you anything true about the version being promoted now; and an owner who is explicitly not the same person as the model's author, enforcing a basic separation-of-duties principle — self-approval defeats the purpose of an independent review requirement. The function returns both a boolean and the specific list of failure reasons rather than just true/false, because a governance gate that fails silently or vaguely forces people to guess what to fix, which erodes trust in the gate and encourages workarounds.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design choice I'd defend here is returning a list of specific failure reasons, not just a boolean. If this gate just says 'denied' with no explanation, people start treating it as an obstacle to route around rather than a real check, and eventually someone finds a way to bypass it entirely. I check for the model card's actual content, not just its existence, because an empty placeholder model card technically satisfies 'a model card exists' while providing none of the governance value it's supposed to provide. I check that the bias evaluation didn't just pass, but passed recently — a stale green checkmark from months ago on a model that's since been retrained isn't evidence of anything about the current model. And the owner check specifically rejects self-approval, because letting the model's own author also be its approving owner defeats the entire point of having an independent sign-off in the approval workflow.
commonMistakes: Checks only for the presence of a model card object, not whether it has meaningful required content
Checks that a bias evaluation exists without checking it passed or how recent it is
Allows the model's author to also serve as its approving owner, defeating separation of duties
Returns only a boolean with no specific failure reasons, making the gate opaque to the team it blocks
keyPoints: Validates model card content, not just presence
Validates bias evaluation status and recency, not just existence
Enforces owner/author separation of duties
Returns specific, actionable failure reasons rather than a bare boolean

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly validates model card content
Correctly validates bias evaluation status and staleness
Correctly enforces owner/author separation of duties
Produces clear, actionable failure output

questions.title: Registering a Data Product in Purview's Unified Catalog
questions.prompt: Walk through, with the concrete fields and metadata you'd set, how you'd register a "Customer 360" data product in Purview's unified catalog so it's discoverable, has an accountable owner, and links clearly to its underlying technical assets.
questions.modelAnswer: Registering a data product correctly means filling in the fields that make it usable by someone who isn't already an expert on it, not just creating a named container. I'd assign it to the correct business domain first (e.g., 'Customer Experience'), since domain assignment is what makes it discoverable in the right context rather than a flat, undifferentiated list. I'd write a description aimed at a business consumer, not a technical one — what questions can this answer, not 'this is a join of five tables.' I'd set an accountable owner field to a specific named person or role (not a team alias with no single accountable individual), since 'who do I ask about this' is one of the most common reasons a catalog entry gets used or ignored. I'd link the underlying technical assets — the actual tables/views that back it — as related assets, so the data product entry serves as the business-facing front door while the technical catalog entries underneath still carry their own schema and lineage detail; the data product shouldn't duplicate that detail, it should point to it. I'd also set status/endorsement fields appropriately (e.g., mark it certified only once it's actually passed review) and tag it with relevant glossary terms so a search for 'customer' surfaces it even if someone doesn't know the product's exact name.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat the data product registration as building the thing a business user actually searches for, as opposed to the technical catalog entries underneath it, which exist for people who already know what they're looking for. So I make sure the business domain is right, because that's what makes search and browse actually work. I write the description in business language — what can you answer with this, not how it's built. I name a real individual or specific role as the owner, not a shared inbox, because the whole point of that field is 'who do I actually ask.' And I explicitly link it to its underlying tables as related assets rather than duplicating their schema details into the data product record, so the data product stays the readable front door and the technical detail stays where it belongs. I'd also tag it with the right glossary terms, because a lot of discovery happens through search, not browsing, and an uncertified, untagged entry might as well not exist to most business users.
commonMistakes: Assigns a shared team alias as owner instead of a specific accountable individual or role
Writes a technical description instead of a business-facing one
Duplicates technical schema/lineage detail into the data product record instead of linking to it
Skips glossary term tagging, making the product hard to discover through search
Marks the product certified before it's actually passed any review

Writes a business-facing description, not a technical one
Assigns a specific, accountable named owner
Links related technical assets rather than duplicating their detail
Uses glossary term tagging and appropriate endorsement status

Assigns a specific, accountable owner correctly
Correctly links underlying technical assets without duplicating detail

questions.title: Propagating a PII Tag to Automatically Mask a Column Across 40 Tables
questions.prompt: Rather than attaching a masking policy to each of 40 tables individually, write the Snowflake SQL that creates a tag, associates a masking policy with that tag, and tags a column so that any column carrying the PII tag across the account is automatically masked.
questions.modelAnswer: Tag-based masking inverts the usual workflow: instead of applying a masking policy to each of 40 columns one at a time, the masking policy is associated once with a tag object via ALTER TAG ... SET MASKING POLICY, and after that, simply tagging any column with that tag (ALTER TABLE ... SET TAG) automatically applies the associated masking policy — no per-column ALTER ... SET MASKING POLICY statement needed for each one. This matters for scale and consistency: a 41st table added next quarter with a phone number column only needs one ALTER TABLE ... SET TAG statement to inherit the same masking behavior automatically, rather than someone having to remember to separately attach a masking policy to it, which is exactly the kind of manual step that gets forgotten at scale. The ALLOWED_VALUES constraint on the tag itself is a quality control: it stops someone from tagging a column with an arbitrary free-text value that wouldn't map to any defined masking behavior. I'd also note this centralizes an audit question nicely — 'which columns are tagged PII and masked' becomes a single query against the tag references system view, rather than requiring someone to check masking policy bindings across 40 separate tables.
questions.professionalAnswer: The whole point of doing it this way is to stop treating masking as a per-table chore. I create one tag, attach the masking policy to the tag itself rather than to any individual table, and from that point forward, tagging a column with that tag is the only step anyone needs to take to get it masked correctly. That means the 41st table someone adds next year doesn't require anyone to remember 'oh, and also go set up masking on this one' — tagging it is the masking setup. I also constrain the tag's allowed values, so someone can't tag a column 'PII-ish' or some other value that doesn't actually map to real masking behavior. And operationally, this gives me a single place to audit coverage — I can query which columns carry this tag account-wide instead of checking 40 tables' masking policy bindings one at a time.
commonMistakes: Applies masking policies directly to each column instead of associating the policy with the tag
Doesn't constrain the tag's allowed values, allowing arbitrary free-text tagging
Misses that tagging a column is the only step needed once the tag-to-policy association exists
Doesn't explain the auditability benefit of centralizing masking through a tag
keyPoints: Correctly creates a tag with constrained allowed values
Correctly associates a masking policy with the tag itself via ALTER TAG
Correctly tags a column to automatically inherit the masking behavior
Explains the scale and audit benefits of this pattern over per-table masking

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct tag creation with constrained allowed values
Correctly associates masking policy with the tag
Correctly tags a column to inherit masking automatically
Explains the scale/audit benefits clearly

questions.title: Writing a Cross-System Consistency Check Between Two 'Authoritative' Sources
questions.prompt: Finance's billing system and the CRM both claim to be authoritative for "active customer count," and leadership wants to know whenever they disagree before it becomes a surprise in a board deck. Write a SQL-based reconciliation check comparing the two systems' daily counts and flagging days where the variance exceeds an agreed threshold.
questions.code:
WITH daily_counts AS (
    SELECT
        c.snapshot_date,
        c.active_customer_count AS crm_count,
        b.active_customer_count AS billing_count
    FROM crm_active_customer_snapshot c
    JOIN billing_active_customer_snapshot b
        ON b.snapshot_date = c.snapshot_date
)
SELECT
    snapshot_date,
    crm_count,
    billing_count,
    ABS(crm_count - billing_count) AS absolute_variance,
    CAST(ABS(crm_count - billing_count) AS DECIMAL(10,4)) / NULLIF(billing_count, 0) * 100 AS pct_variance
FROM daily_counts
WHERE CAST(ABS(crm_count - billing_count) AS DECIMAL(10,4)) / NULLIF(billing_count, 0) * 100 > 2.0  -- agreed threshold
ORDER BY snapshot_date DESC;
questions.modelAnswer: This check deliberately compares percentage variance rather than absolute variance alone, because a fixed absolute threshold doesn't scale sensibly as the customer base grows — a 50-customer gap is alarming at a base of 500 and noise at a base of 500,000, so percentage variance against an agreed threshold (here, 2%) is the more durable rule, with NULLIF guarding against a divide-by-zero on a day billing reports zero. The join assumes both systems have a comparable daily snapshot table at the same grain; a real implementation would need to confirm both sides define 'active' identically before this check is even meaningful — if CRM counts 'active' as logged in within 90 days and billing counts it as 'has a non-canceled subscription,' this query will flag real variance every single day for a reason that isn't a data quality bug, it's a definitional mismatch that needs to be resolved as policy, not patched in SQL. The point of this check isn't to declare a winner between the two systems — it's to surface the days worth investigating, so the output is a candidate list for a human (or a documented business rule) to adjudicate, feeding into the broader authoritative-source-designation process rather than replacing it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as a percentage-variance check, not a flat absolute-number check, because a fixed threshold like 'flag anything over 50' breaks the moment the customer base grows past a certain size — it'll either go permanently silent or permanently noisy. Two percent of the smaller number is a threshold that actually scales with the business. But I'd be upfront with leadership before I even ship this: this query tells you when the two systems disagree, it doesn't tell you who's right, and if 'active' is literally defined differently in CRM versus billing, this will flag variance every day for a reason that has nothing to do with broken data — it's a policy gap, not a bug, and the fix for that is agreeing on one definition, not tuning my threshold. I'd present the output as a daily exception list for someone to actually look at, not as an automated verdict.
commonMistakes: Uses a fixed absolute-count threshold that doesn't scale as the business grows
Doesn't guard against divide-by-zero when computing percentage variance
Treats the check as declaring which system is 'right' rather than surfacing disagreement for investigation
Doesn't flag the risk that the two systems may define 'active' differently, which a SQL check alone can't resolve
keyPoints: Uses percentage variance against an agreed threshold rather than a fixed absolute number
Correctly guards against divide-by-zero
Frames the output as a candidate list for investigation, not an automated verdict
Flags the risk of a definitional mismatch underlying the variance, distinct from a data bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working reconciliation SQL using percentage variance
Correctly guards against edge cases (divide-by-zero)
Frames output appropriately as investigation candidates, not a verdict
Identifies the definitional-mismatch risk distinct from a data quality bug

questions.title: Writing a Drift-Detection Query for a Production Model's Input Features
questions.prompt: Write a SQL query comparing the distribution of a specific feature (customer_age_band) in the last 7 days of production inference requests against its training-data baseline distribution, computing a basic population stability measure, to flag when AI governance monitoring should trigger a model review.
questions.code:
WITH baseline AS (
    SELECT customer_age_band, COUNT(*) * 1.0 / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () AS baseline_pct
    FROM training_data_snapshot
    GROUP BY customer_age_band
),
recent AS (
    SELECT customer_age_band, COUNT(*) * 1.0 / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () AS recent_pct
    FROM production_inference_log
    WHERE inference_date >= DATEADD(day, -7, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))
    GROUP BY customer_age_band
)
SELECT
    b.customer_age_band,
    b.baseline_pct,
    r.recent_pct,
    (r.recent_pct - b.baseline_pct) * LOG(r.recent_pct / b.baseline_pct) AS psi_component
FROM baseline b
JOIN recent r ON r.customer_age_band = b.customer_age_band
ORDER BY psi_component DESC;
-- Sum of psi_component across all bands = Population Stability Index (PSI).
-- PSI < 0.1: no significant drift. 0.1-0.25: moderate, monitor. > 0.25: significant drift, trigger review.
questions.modelAnswer: The Population Stability Index compares a reference distribution (training baseline) against a current distribution (recent production traffic) bucket by bucket, and each bucket's contribution — (recent% − baseline%) × ln(recent% / baseline%) — is designed so that buckets whose share has shifted meaningfully contribute more to the total, while buckets that haven't moved contribute close to zero; summing those contributions gives one interpretable number for the whole feature. I compute both percentages as proportions of their own respective totals (using window functions so each side is normalized independently) specifically so the comparison is apples-to-apples regardless of how many total rows are in the training set versus seven days of production traffic, which will almost always be very different volumes. The published interpretation thresholds (under 0.1 no meaningful drift, 0.1–0.25 worth monitoring, over 0.25 significant enough to trigger a review) are an industry convention, not something this query invents, and I'd use them as the gate for AI governance monitoring to automatically flag a model for review rather than relying on someone remembering to eyeball a chart periodically. One real caveat: PSI on a single feature doesn't tell you the model's actual output or performance has degraded, only that its input distribution has shifted — it's a leading indicator that should trigger investigation, not an automatic conclusion that the model is now wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain PSI as a way of turning 'does this feature's distribution look different now' into one number instead of eyeballing two bar charts side by side. Each age band's contribution gets bigger the more its share of traffic has shifted from training to now, and summing all the bands gives a single score I can put a threshold on. I normalize both sides independently as percentages specifically because the training set and seven days of production traffic are wildly different volumes, and comparing raw counts would be meaningless. I'd wire the standard thresholds — under 0.1 fine, up to 0.25 worth watching, above that trigger a review — into the governance monitoring so this check runs automatically rather than depending on someone remembering to look. And I'd be careful to say out loud that this flags input drift, not necessarily a performance problem — it's the thing that should make us go check performance, not proof that the model's gone wrong.
commonMistakes: Compares raw counts instead of normalized percentages, which breaks when the two datasets have very different volumes
Doesn't know or apply the standard PSI interpretation thresholds
Treats PSI as proof the model's performance has degraded, rather than an input-drift signal that should trigger investigation
Doesn't normalize each side independently (e.g., using a shared denominator incorrectly)
keyPoints: Correctly computes PSI using independently normalized percentages per side
Correctly applies the PSI formula per bucket
Knows and applies the standard interpretation thresholds
Correctly frames PSI as an input-drift signal, not direct proof of performance degradation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working PSI calculation SQL
Correctly normalizes both distributions independently
Correctly applies and explains standard PSI thresholds
Correctly frames the limitation of PSI as an input-drift signal only

questions.title: Nightly Load and Morning Reports Are Deadlocking Each Other
questions.prompt: The nightly ETL load now runs long enough to overlap with early-morning reporting queries, and you're seeing a spike in deadlock errors (1205) exactly in that overlap window. Write the query you'd use to capture the actual deadlock graphs (not just the error count), and describe the architectural fix once you've confirmed the access pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Server Profiler is deprecated, so I'd capture real deadlock graphs through Extended Events — either reading the always-on system_health session's xml_deadlock_report, or standing up a dedicated session — and extract the XML to see exactly which two statements and which objects/lock modes were involved. That turns 'we have deadlocks' into a concrete finding, like 'the ETL's bulk insert into FactOrderSales and a reporting SELECT doing a range scan are colliding on the same rows.' Once that's confirmed, I'd rank the fix options by durability: first, enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT so reporting SELECTs stop taking the shared locks that participate in the deadlock at all, which addresses it structurally rather than by luck of timing; second, shrink and restructure the ETL's transactions so they hold locks for the shortest possible time and touch narrower row ranges, through smaller batches or partition-aligned loads; third, if this keeps recurring, separate the workloads architecturally — widen or shift the load window, or move reporting onto a readable secondary — so the two workloads stop contending for the same locks on the same instance entirely. I'd recommend RCSI as the fast structural win and workload separation as the long-term answer if the overlap keeps growing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't propose a fix off an error count alone — I want the actual deadlock graph first, so I'm pulling it from the system_health Extended Events session rather than reaching for Profiler, which is deprecated at this point. Once I can see exactly which two statements and which rows are colliding, I can say something specific, like 'the nightly bulk insert and a reporting range scan are fighting over the same rows,' instead of just 'we have deadlocks.' From there, my go-to structural fix is read-committed snapshot isolation, because it takes the reporting side out of the locking picture entirely instead of just making it less likely to collide. If the client's really pushing both workloads hard, I'd also talk about shrinking the ETL's transactions and, longer term, moving reporting to a readable secondary — but I'd never reach for NOLOCK as the answer here, because trading a deadlock for a dirty read isn't actually a fix.
questions.example:
-- Query system_health's ring buffer for recent deadlock graphs
SELECT
    xed.value('(event/@timestamp)[1]', 'datetime2') AS EventTime,
    xed.query('.') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file('system_health*.xel', NULL, NULL, NULL) AS f
CROSS APPLY (SELECT CAST(f.event_data AS XML) AS xed) AS d
WHERE xed.value('(event/@name)[1]', 'varchar(100)') = 'xml_deadlock_report'
ORDER BY EventTime DESC;
commonMistakes: Tries to diagnose deadlocks from just the error count/frequency instead of capturing the actual graph
Jumps straight to NOLOCK on the reporting queries as a 'fix', reintroducing dirty-read risk
Only addresses the symptom (overlap timing) without checking whether RCSI would remove the lock conflict structurally
Recommends a replica without first confirming the deadlock is lock-contention, not resource-contention
keyPoints: Uses Extended Events (not deprecated Profiler) to capture real deadlock graphs
Translates the captured graph into a concrete statement-level root cause before proposing a fix
Evaluates RCSI as a structural fix for reader/writer lock conflicts
Considers transaction shrinkage and workload separation (replica) as complementary long-term fixes
Avoids NOLOCK as a quick-fix answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct approach to capturing real deadlock graph evidence
Correctly reasons from captured evidence to root cause
Proposes RCSI or equivalent structural fix with justification
Considers workload separation/transaction design as durable long-term fix

questions.title: A Report Query That Used to Run in 2 Seconds Now Takes Over a Minute
questions.prompt: A nightly report query filtering orders by date has gone from roughly 2 seconds to over a minute as the Orders table grew past 40 million rows. The WHERE clause uses a function on the indexed OrderDate column to normalize it before comparing. Nobody changed the query text or the index. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and provide the corrected query.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd pull the actual execution plan (not estimated) for the query and check whether it's doing an Index Seek or a Scan on OrderDate — on a 40M-row table, a scan where a seek should be possible is the key signal. The WHERE clause wraps the indexed column in CONVERT(date, OrderDate), and applying a function to the column itself makes the predicate non-SARGable: SQL Server can't use the index's sorted order to seek, because it would have to evaluate CONVERT() against every row's OrderDate before it even knows which rows match, forcing a full scan. This likely always technically had this issue, but it only became painfully visible once the table grew enough that scanning became expensive — small tables hide non-SARGable predicates because a full scan is cheap when there's little data. Fix: rewrite the predicate to leave the column bare and move the transformation to the literal side, using a range comparison instead of transforming OrderDate: WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-10-08' AND OrderDate < '2026-10-09'. This lets the optimizer seek directly against the OrderDate index. I'd confirm the fix by re-checking the execution plan for an Index Seek and comparing logical reads/duration before and after.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't start by looking at the index or assuming it got dropped or fragmented — I go get the actual execution plan first, because 'nothing changed' usually means the query had a latent problem the whole time that only became expensive once the table crossed some size. And sure enough, the plan shows a full scan on a 40-million-row table even though there's an index sitting right there on OrderDate. The WHERE clause is the giveaway: CONVERT(date, OrderDate) = '...' wraps the indexed column in a function, and the moment you do that, the optimizer can't use the index's sort order to seek — it has to convert every single row before it can compare anything, so a scan is the only option it has left. This bug was there on day one, it just didn't matter when the table was small enough that a full scan was basically free; growth is what exposed it, not a change to the query or index. The fix is just to stop touching the column and instead express the same filter as a range against the raw OrderDate value. I make the change, pull the plan again, confirm it's an Index Seek now, and compare logical reads before and after so I have real numbers to point to, not just 'it feels faster.'
commonMistakes: Assuming something must have changed (index dropped, stats stale) instead of checking whether the predicate was always non-SARGable
Not pulling the actual execution plan and instead guessing based on query text alone
Rebuilding or adding indexes without first fixing the function-wrapped predicate that prevents any index from being seek-able
Fixing it by wrapping the literal in the same function (CONVERT on both sides) instead of removing the function from the column side entirely
Not validating the fix by comparing before/after execution plans or logical reads
Blaming table growth alone as 'just needs more hardware' instead of identifying the specific non-SARGable predicate
keyPoints: Pulls the actual execution plan to confirm a scan where a seek should be possible
Correctly identifies the function-wrapped column as the SARGability problem
Explains why this was a latent issue exposed by growth rather than a new regression
Rewrites the predicate as a range comparison against the bare column instead of transforming the column
Confirms the fix via execution plan (Index Seek) and reads/duration comparison
Understands that the index itself was never the problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses actual execution plan to diagnose scan vs seek
Correctly identifies non-SARGable predicate as root cause
Corrected SQL properly rewrites as a bare-column range predicate
Validates fix with plan/read comparison

questions.title: A Purview Scan Completes Successfully but New Columns Aren't Classified
questions.prompt: A scheduled Purview scan on a source completes with a green 'Succeeded' status, but a newly-added "SSN" column in one of its tables isn't getting the classification you'd expect, even though the exact same classification rule already correctly tags SSN columns elsewhere. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and the likely causes.
questions.modelAnswer: A 'Succeeded' scan status only confirms the scan completed without an infrastructure-level error — it doesn't mean every table or column was scanned to the depth you expect, so I wouldn't treat it as evidence the classification logic even ran against this column. First I'd check whether this source is on an incremental scan setting rather than a full scan; if so, and if the scan's change-detection didn't register the new column as something requiring re-evaluation (which can happen depending on how the source exposes schema-change metadata), the column may simply never have been scanned for classification at all despite the overall scan reporting success. Second, I'd check the actual scan rule set applied to this specific data source registration — it's common for a source to be registered under a custom scan rule set that doesn't include the classification rule in question, even though that same rule exists and works correctly for other sources using the default or a different custom rule set. Third, I'd check the classification's match thresholds against this column's actual sample data — if the column is sparsely populated or the new rows haven't been sampled yet, the match percentage might fall under the rule's minimum threshold. Fourth, I'd manually trigger a full (not incremental) scan scoped to just this table and inspect the scan's detailed results/classification report, not just the top-level status, to see whether the column was evaluated at all and what it matched against.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd say is that 'Succeeded' doesn't mean what people assume it means — it means the scan job didn't error out, not that every column got evaluated the way we expect. So I check whether this source is set to incremental scanning, because if the scan's change detection didn't pick up the new column as something to re-evaluate, it may have been skipped entirely while the scan still reports success. Then I check the actual scan rule set tied to this specific source registration, because I've seen sources quietly get registered under a custom rule set that's missing a classification rule everyone assumes is just 'on' everywhere. If both of those check out, I look at the actual sample data and match thresholds — a sparsely populated new column might just not have enough matching values yet to cross the confidence bar. And at that point I stop guessing and force a full scan scoped to just that table, then go read the actual classification results in the scan detail, not the status badge.
commonMistakes: Treats a 'Succeeded' scan status as proof the column was actually scanned and evaluated for classification
Doesn't check whether the source is on incremental scanning and whether the new column was detected as a change
Assumes the same scan rule set applies to every source without verifying this specific source's registration
Doesn't check match-percentage thresholds against the column's actual (possibly sparse) sample data
Doesn't force a full scan and inspect detailed classification results before escalating
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes scan 'success' from classification having actually run on this column
Checks incremental vs. full scan behavior and change detection for new columns
Checks whether the correct scan rule set (containing the needed classification) is applied to this specific source
Checks match-threshold behavior against sparse/new sample data
Forces a full scan and inspects detailed results rather than relying on top-level status

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes scan success from classification evaluation
Checks incremental scan/change-detection behavior for new columns
Checks scan rule set assignment on the specific source
Proposes a correct, specific verification step (full scan, detailed results)

questions.title: Lineage Stops at the ADF Pipeline and Doesn't Reach the Destination Table
questions.prompt: In Purview's lineage graph for a pipeline, you can see the source dataset and the Azure Data Factory pipeline itself, but the graph has no edge connecting the pipeline to the destination/sink table — lineage just stops there. Diagnose the likely causes and how you'd resolve each.
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause is that the sink dataset inside the ADF pipeline isn't resolving to the same asset identity Purview already has registered for that table from its own scan of the destination source — lineage requires both ends of an edge to resolve to a consistent asset reference, and if the ADF sink's linked service/dataset path doesn't exactly match how the destination was registered and scanned in Purview (different connection string casing, a different logical server name alias, or the destination not registered as a source at all), Purview has no asset to draw the edge to, so it simply omits it rather than erroring visibly. A second common cause is the activity type: Purview's automatic lineage extraction for ADF supports specific activity types (notably Copy Activity) well, but custom activities, certain Dataflow configurations, or Stored Procedure/Script activities that write to the destination don't get automatic lineage extraction the same way, so if the actual write to the destination happens through one of those, no edge will ever be generated without manual lineage push via the Atlas/Purview API. Third, I'd check whether the destination was ever scanned and registered in Purview's data map at all — lineage can only connect to an asset Purview already knows about; if the destination source was never registered and scanned, there's no asset for the edge to point to regardless of the pipeline configuration. My diagnostic order: confirm the destination is registered and scanned, confirm the activity type supports automatic lineage, then check for an asset-identity mismatch between the ADF sink config and the registered asset.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by checking the most basic thing first: is the destination table even registered as a scanned source in Purview at all? Lineage can only draw a line to an asset Purview already knows exists — if nobody registered and scanned that destination, there's nothing for the pipeline's output to connect to, no matter how the pipeline is built. If it is registered, I'd look at the activity type doing the actual write — Purview's automatic lineage extraction covers Copy Activity well, but some Dataflow setups and anything going through a Stored Procedure or custom script activity often don't get picked up automatically, and that's a frequent reason lineage just stops. If neither of those explains it, I'd dig into whether the sink's connection details in ADF actually resolve to the exact same asset identity Purview registered for that destination — a mismatched server alias or connection string formatting is a sneaky, common reason two things that are 'the same table' don't look like the same asset to Purview's lineage resolution.
commonMistakes: Assumes lineage extraction automatically covers every ADF activity type, including custom/script/certain dataflow activities
Doesn't check whether the destination was ever registered and scanned as a source in Purview at all
Overlooks asset-identity mismatches between the ADF sink configuration and the registered destination asset
Jumps to 'Purview is broken' instead of methodically checking registration, activity type, and identity resolution in order
keyPoints: Checks whether the destination is registered and scanned in Purview's data map at all
Checks whether the specific activity type supports Purview's automatic lineage extraction
Checks for asset-identity mismatches between the ADF sink and the registered destination asset
Follows a logical diagnostic order rather than guessing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly checks destination registration/scanning first
Correctly identifies activity-type lineage support as a cause
Correctly identifies asset-identity mismatch as a cause
Follows a logical, methodical diagnostic order
