questions.title: Finance and Sales Both Claim Authoritative 'Active Customer' Counts That Disagree by 12%
questions.prompt: Finance's billing system and Sales's CRM both claim authoritative status for "active customer count," and they disagree by roughly 12% every month. Leadership wants an answer to "which one is right." Walk through the diagnostic approach you'd actually take before declaring a winner, and how you'd resolve the authoritative-source question going forward.
questions.modelAnswer: I would not start by trying to figure out which system is 'wrong,' because a consistent 12% gap, month after month, is a strong signal this isn't a data quality defect at all — it's much more likely that the two systems are each correctly implementing two different definitions of 'active.' My first step is to get both systems' actual business logic in writing: what specific condition does billing's query use to mark a customer active (e.g., has a non-canceled subscription with a charge in the last 30 days), and what condition does the CRM use (e.g., logged in or had any sales activity within 90 days) — nine times out of ten, a definitional mismatch like this fully explains a stable, repeating percentage gap, whereas a genuine data quality bug tends to produce an inconsistent or growing gap, not a steady one. Once I've confirmed it's definitional, declaring one system 'right' is the wrong framing — both are right under their own definition. The real fix is a governance decision, not a technical one: convene the actual business owners of 'active customer' as a concept, agree on one canonical definition (or explicitly agree there are two valid metrics that need two distinct, clearly-labeled names, like 'billing-active' and 'engagement-active'), document that definition in the business glossary, and formally designate one system as authoritative for that specific metric going forward, with the other system's number either retired from that context or clearly relabeled so it's never again presented as the same thing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd resist the urge to immediately dig into one system's SQL looking for a bug, because a steady, repeating 12% gap month after month doesn't look like a data quality problem to me — it looks like two correct answers to two different questions. So my first move is getting both teams' actual definitions of 'active' in front of me, in writing, not a two-minute Slack explanation. Almost always, that's where the gap lives — billing might mean 'has an active paid subscription,' CRM might mean 'had any engagement in the last quarter,' and both numbers are completely correct for what they're each measuring. Once that's confirmed, I don't go back to leadership with 'system X is right' — I go back with 'these are two different metrics that have been wearing the same name,' and the actual fix is a governance conversation: get the business owners in a room, agree on one canonical definition or two clearly distinct names, write it into the glossary, and formally pick an authoritative source for whichever definition the business actually needs for this reporting context.
commonMistakes: Immediately assumes one system has a bug and starts debugging its SQL/ETL without first checking definitions
Declares a 'winner' without confirming whether the two numbers are even measuring the same thing
Treats this as a purely technical problem instead of recognizing it needs a business/governance decision
Fixes it informally (a one-off explanation to leadership) instead of documenting the resolved definition in the glossary and formally designating an authoritative source
keyPoints: Recognizes a stable, repeating percentage gap as a signal of definitional mismatch, not a data bug
Investigates and compares the actual business logic/definition each system uses before touching code
Reframes 'which is right' into a governance decision about definitions, not a technical debugging exercise
Resolves it durably: documents the agreed definition in the glossary and formally designates an authoritative source

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses a stable gap as likely definitional, not a quality bug
Describes the correct investigative approach (comparing actual business logic/definitions)
Correctly reframes the problem as a governance decision, not a technical one
Proposes a durable resolution (glossary documentation, authoritative source designation)

questions.title: A User Has Catalog-Level SELECT but Still Can't Query a Specific Table
questions.prompt: A user reports that even though they were explicitly granted SELECT at the catalog level in Unity Catalog, they still get a permission-denied error querying one specific table inside it. Diagnose the likely cause and the correct fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The near-universal cause of this specific symptom is a missing privilege in the chain Unity Catalog actually requires, not a problem with the SELECT grant itself. Unity Catalog's permission model requires USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the containing schema in addition to SELECT on the table — USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA don't grant the ability to see or query data by themselves, but without them, a user cannot even 'enter' the catalog or schema to reach a table they do have SELECT on, no matter how that SELECT was granted. Many admins grant SELECT broadly at the catalog level, assuming that single grant is sufficient, without realizing catalog-level SELECT does inherit down to tables by default in most configurations but USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA are separate privileges that must also be granted, and they're commonly forgotten because they don't show up as intuitively necessary — they feel like plumbing rather than a real permission. The fix is to check (SHOW GRANTS) whether the user's role actually has USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the specific schema containing the problem table, and grant whichever is missing; if SELECT was only granted at the catalog level and the behavior differs for this one table, I'd also check for an explicit REVOKE at the table or schema level that could override the inherited catalog grant for this specific object.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always the same root cause when I see it: someone granted SELECT thinking that was the whole permission, but Unity Catalog actually needs a chain — USE CATALOG, then USE SCHEMA, then the actual object-level privilege — and USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA don't feel like 'real' permissions to grant because they don't let you see any data by themselves, so they get forgotten. So my first move is SHOW GRANTS against the catalog and the specific schema for this user's role, checking specifically for USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, not just SELECT. If those are missing, that's the fix — grant them. If they're actually present and it's still failing on this one specific table, then I'd check whether someone explicitly revoked something at the table or schema level that's overriding the broader catalog grant for just this object, because that's the other common way 'I granted it at the catalog level' doesn't behave the way someone expects for one particular table.
commonMistakes: Assumes SELECT alone should be sufficient and doesn't check for USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA
Re-grants SELECT repeatedly without diagnosing the actual missing privilege in the chain
Doesn't check for a table- or schema-level REVOKE that could override a broader catalog-level grant
Doesn't use SHOW GRANTS to actually verify what privileges exist before guessing
keyPoints: Correctly identifies missing USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA as the near-universal cause
Explains why these privileges are easy to forget despite being required
Uses SHOW GRANTS to verify the actual privilege chain rather than guessing
Checks for an overriding REVOKE at a lower level as a secondary cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA requirement as the likely cause
Explains the privilege chain mechanics accurately
Proposes correct diagnostic steps (SHOW GRANTS)
Considers a secondary cause (overriding REVOKE)

questions.title: A User's Role Has the Right Grants but Every Query Still Fails With 'Insufficient Privileges'
questions.prompt: A Snowflake user insists their role has been granted all the right privileges — and a check confirms it has — but every query they run still fails with insufficient privileges. Diagnose the likely cause and how you'd confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause of exactly this symptom is that the privileges exist on the role, but that role isn't the user's active role in the current session — Snowflake users can be granted multiple roles, but only one role is active per session at a time (the user's default role, or whatever they explicitly switched to with USE ROLE), and querying against privileges that belong to a different, inactive granted role fails with an insufficient-privileges error that looks identical to the role genuinely lacking the grant. I'd confirm this by having the user run SELECT CURRENT_ROLE() to see what's actually active in their session, compare it against the role the privileges were actually granted to, and if they don't match, have them run USE ROLE <correct_role> before retrying — if that resolves it, the root cause was confirmed to be an inactive-role mismatch, not a missing grant. A related but distinct cause worth checking if role-switching doesn't fix it: the role's grants might exist but not have been propagated correctly through the role hierarchy if the privilege was granted to a different role that was supposed to be granted to this one but wasn't actually linked — in which case SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE <role> on the role actually active in session is the way to verify what it genuinely has, rather than trusting a check performed against a different role.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I go anywhere near re-checking grants, I ask the user to run SELECT CURRENT_ROLE() and tell me exactly what comes back, because this symptom — 'the role definitely has the right grants, but it still fails' — is almost always a session using a different role than the one that was actually checked. Snowflake users often have several roles granted to them, but only one is active in a session at a time, and if nobody explicitly switched roles, they might be sitting on their default role while the privileges live on a different role they were also granted. If CURRENT_ROLE() doesn't match the role that actually has the privileges, I have them run USE ROLE to the correct one and try again — that resolves the vast majority of these. If it still fails after confirming the active role is correct, then I actually go verify with SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE against that specific active role, because at that point I want to see what it has for real, not trust a check that might have been run against the wrong role in the first place.
commonMistakes: Re-verifies the grant repeatedly without checking which role is actually active in the user's session
Assumes 'the role has the grant' and 'the session is using that role' are the same thing
Doesn't use CURRENT_ROLE() to confirm the active role before escalating further
Doesn't re-verify grants with SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE against the actually-active role if the issue persists
keyPoints: Correctly identifies active-role-vs-granted-role mismatch as the most likely cause
Uses CURRENT_ROLE() to diagnose the mismatch
Proposes USE ROLE as the immediate fix if confirmed
Falls back to SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE against the correct active role if the issue persists

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the active-role mismatch as the likely cause
Proposes the correct diagnostic (CURRENT_ROLE())
Proposes the correct fix (USE ROLE)
Considers a secondary verification step if the first fix doesn't resolve it

questions.title: RLS Filters Correctly in Desktop but Shows All Rows for Everyone in the Service
questions.prompt: Row-level security filters correctly when testing roles in Power BI Desktop, but once published, several users report seeing all rows in the Power BI service regardless of the RLS role assigned. Diagnose the likely causes.
questions.modelAnswer: The single most common cause of this exact symptom is workspace role: RLS does not apply to users who are Members, Contributors, or Admins of the workspace the report lives in — those roles are treated as having full access to the underlying data regardless of any RLS role assignment, by design, because workspace-level roles are a broader permission than report-level RLS. If the affected users were added as workspace Members for convenience (a very common shortcut), RLS will correctly appear to do nothing for them, and this is not a bug, it's expected behavior that needs addressing by moving those users to the Viewer role and controlling their actual report access through an app or direct share instead. Second, I'd check whether 'Test as role' in Desktop was used to validate the logic (which simulates the filter locally) versus actually publishing the role assignments and mapping real Azure AD users/groups to those roles in the Service — a role can be perfectly correct in Desktop and simply never have real users mapped to it after publish, in which case nobody has any RLS role applied and default (unfiltered, if no role catches them) behavior applies. Third, if this is a DirectQuery or live connection scenario against a source that itself doesn't enforce the same row security, RLS defined only in the Power BI semantic model won't protect data accessed another way, though that's less likely to present as 'all rows showing in the Power BI service' specifically.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch the DAX, I check workspace roles, because this is the single most common reason RLS looks broken in production — if the affected users are workspace Members, Contributors, or Admins rather than Viewers, Power BI doesn't apply RLS to them at all, by design, since those roles already imply broader access. That's usually exactly what's happening: someone added people as Members for convenience, and now RLS correctly isn't doing anything to them. Second thing I check is whether the role-to-user mapping actually got set up after publishing, separate from testing it in Desktop with 'Test as role' — that only simulates locally, it doesn't create the real security-group-to-role assignment in the Service, and I've seen teams validate the logic perfectly and then simply forget that step. I'd fix the workspace roles first, since that's the more likely culprit, before assuming the RLS definition itself is broken.
commonMistakes: Assumes the RLS DAX logic itself is broken without first checking workspace roles
Doesn't know RLS is not applied to workspace Members/Contributors/Admins
Confuses 'Test as role' validation in Desktop with actual role-to-user mapping after publish
Doesn't check whether real users/groups were ever actually assigned to the RLS roles in the Service
keyPoints: Correctly identifies workspace role (Member/Contributor/Admin) as bypassing RLS entirely
Correctly distinguishes Desktop 'Test as role' simulation from real post-publish role assignment
Checks whether real users/groups were actually mapped to RLS roles in the Service
Diagnoses in the correct priority order (most likely cause first)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies workspace role as the most likely cause
Correctly explains why workspace roles bypass RLS
Correctly distinguishes Desktop testing from Service role mapping
Diagnoses in a sensible priority order

questions.title: Workspaces Keep Appearing Outside Any Domain, Breaking the Governance Model
questions.prompt: Your Fabric domain-based governance model assigns every workspace to a domain so classification, ownership, and policy apply consistently. New workspaces keep showing up unassigned to any domain. Diagnose why this keeps happening and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: If workspace-to-domain assignment is a manual, after-the-fact step rather than an enforced part of workspace creation, new workspaces will inevitably accumulate outside any domain simply because self-service creation is faster and more common than anyone remembering to go assign a domain afterward — this is a process gap, not a tooling failure, and it will keep recurring regardless of how many times existing workspaces are manually reassigned. The specific fix is at the tenant admin level: Fabric's admin portal has tenant settings governing domain assignment, including the ability to restrict who can create workspaces and, more importantly, domain contributor settings that can allow domain admins to automatically claim/assign workspaces matching certain criteria (such as a naming convention or the creator's security group) into their domain at creation time, rather than relying on manual post-hoc assignment. I'd also check whether workspace creation itself is unrestricted tenant-wide — if anyone can create a workspace with no required attribute or naming convention tying it to a domain, there's nothing for even an automated assignment rule to match against. The durable fix is two-layered: enforce a naming convention or required metadata at creation (so domain assignment has something to key off), and configure domain-level auto-assignment rules so new matching workspaces are captured automatically rather than requiring a human to notice and act.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this as a process problem before a tooling problem — if assigning a workspace to a domain is something a human has to remember to do after the fact, it will not keep up with however many workspaces get created, full stop. So the real fix is making domain assignment automatic, not manually diligent. In the Fabric admin portal, domain admins can set up rules that automatically claim workspaces into their domain based on things like naming convention or the creator's group, so a new workspace lands in the right domain at creation time instead of needing someone to notice it's drifting unassigned. But that only works if there's something consistent to match against, so I'd also push for a required naming convention or workspace creation process that ties every new workspace to a domain signal from day one. I wouldn't just do another manual sweep to reassign the current stragglers — that fixes today's backlog and guarantees next month's backlog looks the same.
commonMistakes: Proposes another manual cleanup sweep without addressing why new unassigned workspaces keep appearing
Doesn't know Fabric supports automated domain-assignment rules for domain admins
Doesn't connect the lack of a naming convention/required metadata to the automated rule having nothing to match against
Treats this purely as a tooling limitation rather than a process/enforcement gap
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses this as a process gap (manual assignment doesn't scale), not a tooling failure
Identifies Fabric's automated domain-assignment capability as the real fix
Connects a required naming convention/metadata to making automated assignment possible
Avoids proposing only a one-time manual cleanup as a durable fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the root cause as a process/enforcement gap
Identifies automated domain-assignment rules as the fix
Connects naming convention/metadata requirements to enabling automation
Avoids a non-durable, manual-only fix

questions.title: A Production Model's Approval Rate for a Demographic Group Jumped 15 Points Overnight
questions.prompt: Your AI governance monitoring flags that a production credit-approval model's approval rate for one demographic group jumped 15 percentage points overnight, with no model deployment in that window. Walk through your incident-response triage sequence before deciding on rollback, investigation, or retraining.
questions.modelAnswer: A sudden overnight shift with no model deployment rules out the model itself as the change, which narrows the real question to: what changed upstream. My triage sequence, in order: first, check the upstream data pipeline for a bug or schema change — a feature that silently started receiving nulls, a unit change, a join that started duplicating or dropping rows, or an upstream source outage that got backfilled with defaults, are all far more common causes of a sudden metric jump than genuine population or policy drift, and this should be checked before anything else because it's both the most likely cause and the easiest to disprove or confirm quickly. Second, check whether a genuine, documented business or policy change happened in that window — a credit policy threshold change, a promotional campaign targeting that demographic, or an eligibility rule change — since a real, intended change can look identical to a data bug in the raw numbers but requires a completely different response. Third, if neither a pipeline bug nor a known policy change explains it, treat it as a potential real drift event and pull the actual feature distributions for that window to see which inputs shifted. Only after ruling out a pipeline bug and confirming no intended policy change would I consider this a genuine model behavior change worth escalating toward rollback (if the shift is clearly erroneous and harmful) or a full fairness re-evaluation and potential retraining (if it's real and concerning) — jumping straight to retraining or rollback before this triage risks either masking a pipeline bug that will recur, or overreacting to an intended business change.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I will not do is retrain or roll back before I understand what actually happened, because a 15-point overnight jump with no deployment screams 'something upstream changed,' not 'the model suddenly started behaving differently on its own.' So step one is the data pipeline — I'm looking for a feature that started coming through null, a schema change, a broken join, anything that would shift the model's inputs without anyone touching the model. Step two, in parallel, is checking whether there was an intentional business change in that window — a policy threshold, a new campaign — because that can produce a real, correct shift that looks alarming out of context but isn't actually a governance problem, it's a communication gap. Only if both of those come back clean do I start treating this as a genuine model behavior or drift event worth a real fairness investigation, and only after that investigation would retraining or rollback even be on the table. Reacting before triage risks either missing a pipeline bug that'll just happen again, or treating an intended business decision as a model failure.
commonMistakes: Jumps straight to retraining or rolling back the model before investigating upstream causes
Doesn't check for an upstream data pipeline bug as the first, most likely explanation
Doesn't check whether an intentional business/policy change explains the shift before treating it as a model problem
Treats a sudden metric jump as automatically indicating real population drift without ruling out simpler explanations first
keyPoints: Correctly rules out the model itself as the source of change given no deployment occurred
Checks for an upstream data pipeline bug as the first, most likely cause
Checks for an intentional, documented business/policy change as a parallel explanation
Only escalates to real drift investigation and potential retraining/rollback after ruling out simpler causes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes upstream data/pipeline investigation first
Checks for intentional business/policy changes before assuming a model problem
Follows a logical triage order before deciding on rollback/retraining
Avoids overreacting (premature retraining/rollback) before triage completes

questions.title: Lineage Disappears the Moment Data Crosses From AWS S3 Into Azure
questions.prompt: Your lineage graph correctly tracks data within AWS (S3 to Glue to Redshift) and separately within Azure (ADLS to Synapse to Power BI), but the moment a dataset is transferred from the AWS side to the Azure side, lineage shows a dead end — the Azure-side asset appears with no connection back to its AWS origin. Diagnose why, and how you'd re-establish the bridge.
questions.modelAnswer: Each cloud's native and governance tooling tracks lineage within its own platform boundary using that platform's own asset-identity model — AWS-side tools resolve lineage against Glue Catalog/S3 asset identifiers, Azure-side tools (including Purview scanning ADLS/Synapse) resolve against Azure Resource Manager-style identifiers — and neither has an inherent concept of the other's asset identity, so there is no native mechanism connecting 'this S3 object' to 'this ADLS file it was copied into' unless something explicitly tells the lineage system they're the same logical dataset. The transfer itself is almost certainly happening through a process — a scheduled copy job, Data Factory's copy activity reading from S3, or a manual/ad hoc transfer script — that either isn't registered as a lineage-aware activity in Purview (if it's a custom script or a tool outside Purview's automatic extraction scope) or is technically visible to Purview on the Azure side but has no visibility into the AWS-side source asset at all, since Purview's own scanning of AWS resources requires AWS sources to be separately registered and scanned into the same data map. The fix is to explicitly bridge the two: register the AWS-side S3/Glue source into Purview's data map (so it has an asset identity Purview recognizes) if it isn't already, and ensure the actual transfer mechanism either is a lineage-extraction-supported activity (such as an ADF/Synapse pipeline copy activity with both source and sink registered) or, if it's a custom process, push lineage explicitly via the Purview Atlas API connecting the two registered asset GUIDs — cross-cloud lineage essentially never happens automatically without one unified catalog aware of both sides and an explicit or supported mechanism recording the transfer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as a consequence of each side only knowing about its own world. AWS-native tooling understands S3 and Glue identities; Azure-side tooling understands ADLS and Synapse identities; neither one has a built-in concept of the other, so unless something explicitly bridges them, there's no reason to expect a connected line across that boundary — this isn't a bug, it's the absence of a mechanism that was never built. The practical fix starts with getting the AWS-side source registered and scanned into the same catalog (Purview, in most of my client environments) that's already tracking the Azure side, so there's at least one place that knows about both assets. Then I look at how the actual transfer happens — if it's going through something like an ADF copy activity with both ends registered, Purview can often pick up that edge automatically; if it's a custom script or an outside tool, I'd push the lineage edge explicitly through the Purview API, connecting the two asset identities directly, because nothing is going to infer that connection on its own across two different clouds' native identity systems.
commonMistakes: Assumes a lineage/catalog tool should automatically bridge cross-cloud asset identities without any explicit connection
Doesn't check whether the AWS-side source is even registered in the same catalog as the Azure side
Doesn't distinguish between a lineage-extraction-supported transfer mechanism and a custom/unsupported one
Doesn't consider pushing lineage explicitly via an API when the transfer mechanism isn't natively supported
keyPoints: Correctly explains that each cloud's tooling has no native concept of the other's asset identity
Identifies the need to register the AWS-side source into the same unified catalog as the Azure side
Distinguishes supported transfer mechanisms (auto lineage) from unsupported ones (requiring explicit API push)
Proposes a concrete bridging mechanism rather than expecting automatic cross-cloud resolution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why cross-cloud lineage doesn't resolve automatically
Identifies the need for unified catalog registration of both sides
Distinguishes supported vs. unsupported transfer mechanisms correctly
Proposes a concrete, workable bridging fix

questions.title: Stewards Are Nominally Assigned but Nobody Is Doing the Work Six Months In
questions.prompt: Six months after launching your stewardship program, every critical data element has a named steward on paper, but quality issues sit unresolved for weeks, glossary terms go unreviewed, and stewards say they 'haven't had time.' Diagnose the likely root causes of this stalled program and the fix sequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Having a name on a stewardship assignment and having a functioning program are different things, and the gap between them is almost always explained by one or more of three root causes, which I'd check in order of likelihood. First, and most common: stewardship was added as an unfunded extra duty on top of stewards' actual day jobs, with no time formally allocated and no adjustment to their existing workload or performance goals — if a steward's manager never agreed their team member would spend real hours on this, 'I haven't had time' isn't an excuse, it's an accurate description of a program that was never actually resourced. Second: there's no visible consequence or incentive tied to doing the work versus not doing it — if nothing observably changes whether a steward actively works issues or lets them sit, rational people deprioritize unrewarded work under real deadline pressure. Third: stewards may genuinely not know what 'doing the work' looks like day to day — if onboarding covered the concept of stewardship but never walked through the actual weekly cadence (what to review, what tool to use, what a resolved issue looks like), the role is clear in title only. I'd diagnose by interviewing a sample of stewards directly rather than assuming, then sequence the fix: first get explicit time allocation agreed with their managers (this is a negotiation the governance program owner needs to have, not something stewards can fix themselves), then build a lightweight, concrete weekly routine, then add visibility (a simple dashboard of open vs. resolved items per steward) so engagement becomes observable rather than invisible.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't guess at this — I'd actually go talk to five or six of the stewards and ask them directly what's stopping them, because the answer usually clusters into one of a few things, and the fix is different depending on which it is. Most often, it's that nobody actually carved out time for this — stewardship got layered on top of an existing full workload with no adjustment, so 'I haven't had time' is just true, not an excuse, and no amount of encouragement fixes that; it needs their managers to formally agree to real time allocation, which is a conversation I have to go have, not something I can fix by emailing the stewards harder. Sometimes it's that nothing visibly changes whether they engage or not, so it quietly becomes the first thing to slip under pressure — in that case I'd add a simple visibility mechanism, even something as basic as a dashboard showing open items per steward, so the work stops being invisible. And sometimes people genuinely don't know what 'being a steward' means week to week, in which case the fix is a concrete routine, not a renewed appeal to the importance of the role.
commonMistakes: Assumes stewards are simply uncommitted or careless rather than investigating structural causes
Doesn't check whether real time was ever formally allocated for the role versus added as unfunded extra work
Responds with more reminders/communication instead of addressing the lack of time allocation or visibility
Doesn't interview actual stewards to understand the real blocker before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Diagnoses via direct interviews rather than assumption
Identifies lack of formal time allocation as the most common root cause
Identifies lack of visibility/consequence as a second common cause
Identifies unclear day-to-day expectations as a third cause, and sequences fixes appropriately (time allocation before routine/visibility)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes investigating via direct conversation rather than assuming the cause
Correctly identifies lack of time allocation as the most likely root cause
Identifies visibility/incentive and clarity-of-expectations as additional causes
Proposes a sensible fix sequence

questions.title: A Masking Policy Is Attached but a Role That Should Be Masked Is Seeing Plaintext
questions.prompt: A Snowflake masking policy is confirmed attached to a column, but a role that should see masked data is seeing the real, unmasked values. Diagnose the likely causes.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd check is whether the role seeing unmasked data is actually the role the masking policy's conditional logic checks, versus the role the user thinks they're using — the same active-role-versus-granted-role confusion that affects general privilege troubleshooting applies here too, so if the masking policy's CASE logic checks CURRENT_ROLE() against specific named roles and the user's session is on a different active role than expected, the comparison might accidentally evaluate to the unmasking branch. Second, and very commonly the actual cause: the data is being accessed through a view that was created before the masking policy was attached, or that queries the base table in a way (like SELECT * materialized into a different object, or a view owned by a role with elevated privileges) that bypasses the masking evaluation — masking policies evaluate based on the querying context, and a view can sometimes present data differently than a direct table query depending on how it's defined and who owns it, so I'd check whether the access path is actually the masked table directly or an intermediary object. Third, I'd check whether grants changed after the policy was written — if the policy's logic was written referencing a role that was since renamed, dropped and recreated, or whose hierarchy changed, the comparison might silently stop matching as intended. My diagnostic order: confirm active role in session, confirm the exact access path (direct table vs. view), then re-verify the policy's actual logic against current role names.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start exactly where I'd start for a general privilege mismatch: what role is actually active in this session, and does it match what the masking policy's logic is checking for? If the policy's CASE statement is comparing CURRENT_ROLE() against a specific role name and the session is on a different active role than expected, the masking condition can land on the wrong branch without anyone's grants being 'wrong' in any obvious way. If that checks out, my next suspect is the access path — is this role actually querying the masked table directly, or going through a view that predates the masking policy or behaves differently because of how it was defined or who owns it? I've seen masking policies applied correctly to a base table while an older view sitting on top of it quietly keeps showing the original behavior. And if both of those are clean, I go back and literally re-read the policy's logic against the current, real role names, because roles get renamed or recreated more often than people remember to update policy logic that references them by name.
commonMistakes: Assumes the masking policy itself must be broken without checking the active role in session first
Doesn't check whether the access path is a view that bypasses or predates the masking policy
Doesn't consider that role renames/recreation could silently break a policy's hardcoded role-name logic
Re-attaches or rewrites the masking policy before diagnosing the actual access path and role context
keyPoints: Checks active-role-versus-expected-role mismatch in the masking policy's logic
Checks whether the access path (view vs. direct table) bypasses the masking evaluation
Checks for stale role-name references in the policy logic after role changes
Follows a logical diagnostic order

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly checks active-role mismatch against the policy's logic
Correctly identifies view/access-path bypass as a likely cause
Considers stale role-name references as a cause
Follows a logical, methodical diagnostic order

questions.title: Two Business Domains Defined 'Customer' Differently in the Glossary, and Reports Disagree
questions.prompt: You discover that two business domains in Purview's unified catalog each created their own glossary term for "Customer" with materially different definitions, and reports built against each disagree as a result. Diagnose the governance process gap that let this happen, and the remediation — not just picking a winner.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a process gap, not a Purview limitation: if domains can independently create glossary terms with no cross-domain duplicate-check or shared-term review step, two domains creating overlapping terms for a widely-used business concept is inevitable, especially for a term as universal as 'Customer' that multiple domains legitimately interact with from different angles. The underlying cause is almost always that domain-level glossary authority was granted without a governing rule for terms that span multiple domains — each domain owner reasonably believed they had the authority to define 'Customer' for their own context, and nothing in the process required checking whether the term already existed elsewhere before creating it. The remediation is not to simply pick one definition and delete the other, because both domains likely built real reporting logic on their respective definition, and an abrupt unilateral change breaks their reports without warning; instead, convene both domain's business owners together, determine whether this is genuinely one concept that needs one shared definition (in which case it becomes a cross-domain or enterprise-level glossary term, with both domains' reporting eventually migrated to reference it) or whether they're actually describing two legitimately distinct concepts that happen to share a name (in which case both terms should be renamed to be unambiguous, e.g., 'Billing Customer' and 'Engagement Customer', so the catalog never again presents two different things under one identical label). The process fix going forward is a mandatory duplicate-term check before approving any new glossary term, with any term matching or overlapping an existing one routed to a cross-domain review rather than approved unilaterally by a single domain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't frame the fix as 'which definition wins,' because that's going to make one domain feel like their established, working definition just got overruled, and it skips the real question of whether these are even describing the same thing. My first step is getting both domain owners in the same room to work that out together — sometimes 'Customer' really is one concept that needs one shared definition, and sometimes it turns out they're describing two genuinely different things that happen to share a label, in which case the fix is just renaming both terms to be specific, not merging them. Either way, the deeper issue is the process gap that let this happen in the first place — nothing required checking whether a term already existed before a domain created its own version of it. So alongside resolving this specific collision, I'd push for a mandatory duplicate-check step before any new glossary term gets approved, so a widely-relevant term like this gets routed to a cross-domain review instead of being created unilaterally next time.
commonMistakes: Jumps to declaring one domain's definition correct and deleting the other without reconciling the underlying reporting
Doesn't investigate whether the two domains are actually describing the same concept or two legitimately distinct ones
Treats this as a one-time glossary cleanup without fixing the process gap that allowed duplicate terms to be created unilaterally
Doesn't involve both domains' actual business owners in the resolution
keyPoints: Diagnoses the root cause as a missing duplicate-term check/cross-domain review process, not a tooling flaw
Avoids unilaterally picking a winner without reconciling downstream reporting impact
Determines whether the two terms describe one shared concept or two legitimately distinct ones
Proposes a durable process fix (mandatory duplicate-check/cross-domain review for new terms)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the governance process gap, not a tooling issue
Avoids a unilateral 'pick a winner' resolution
Correctly determines same-concept vs. distinct-concept resolution path
Proposes a durable forward-looking process fix

questions.title: A Required-Tag Policy Keeps Letting Resources Slip Through in One Subscription
questions.prompt: You've assigned an Azure Policy requiring a 'DataClassification' tag at the management group level with a Deny effect, yet resources in one specific subscription keep being created without the tag. Diagnose the likely causes.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd check, in order, the places a management-group-level policy's effect can be overridden or weakened for one specific scope. First, policy exemptions: Azure allows specific resources or an entire subscription to be explicitly exempted from a policy assignment, and if someone created an exemption for this subscription (even temporarily, for a migration or legacy workload) and never removed it, every resource in it would correctly bypass the Deny effect exactly as configured — this is the most common cause of 'the policy works everywhere except here.' Second, I'd check whether a policy assignment exists at the subscription level itself that effectively overrides or duplicates the management-group assignment with a different effect (e.g., an old assignment set to Audit that's technically a separate assignment rather than an override, but creates confusion about which is 'in effect' — Azure Policy effects from multiple matching assignments are generally cumulative/most-restrictive, so this is less likely to cause slip-through but worth ruling out). Third, and worth checking directly: whether this subscription sits in a different management group branch than assumed — if the org's management group hierarchy doesn't actually place this subscription under the management group the policy was assigned to, the policy was never in scope for it at all, which is a very common 'the hierarchy isn't what I assumed' mistake. Fourth, resources created via a deployment method that uses a service principal with elevated bypass permissions, or resources created before the policy assignment existed and never remediated via a remediation task, would also show as non-compliant without technically 'slipping through' a live Deny — I'd distinguish pre-existing non-compliant resources from genuinely new ones bypassing Deny right now.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is checking for a policy exemption on that subscription, because that's the single most common reason a Deny policy that clearly works everywhere else doesn't work in one specific place — someone exempted it, often for a legitimate short-term reason like a migration, and the exemption just never got cleaned up. If there's no exemption, I check the management group hierarchy itself, because it's a surprisingly common mistake to assume a subscription sits under a management group it actually doesn't — if it's not really in scope, the policy was never going to apply to it regardless of the assignment being correct everywhere else. I'd also separate out whether we're talking about genuinely new resources bypassing a live Deny right now, versus older non-compliant resources that were created before the policy existed and just never got swept up by a remediation task — those look the same in a compliance report but have completely different fixes.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check for a policy exemption on the specific subscription
Assumes the management group hierarchy places the subscription in scope without verifying it
Confuses pre-existing non-compliant resources (needing remediation) with resources actively bypassing a live Deny
Doesn't distinguish Deny-effect bypass from Audit-effect resources that were simply never remediated
keyPoints: Checks for a policy exemption on the specific subscription as the most likely cause
Verifies the actual management group hierarchy placement for the subscription
Distinguishes genuinely bypassing new resources from pre-existing non-remediated ones
Investigates in a logical, prioritized order

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies policy exemption as the most likely cause
Correctly checks management group hierarchy placement
Correctly distinguishes new bypass vs. pre-existing non-remediated resources
Investigates in a logical, prioritized order

questions.title: Design a Star Schema With Type 2 History for a New Subject Area
questions.prompt: The client wants a new 'Employee Performance' subject area added to their existing warehouse, with full historical tracking of employee department/title changes over time, and fast year-over-year aggregate reporting. As the architect, design the star schema (fact + dimension DDL sketch) and explain how SCD Type 2 and surrogate keys fit together to make this correct.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd design one fact table, FactEmployeePerformance, at the grain of one row per employee per review period, surrounded by DimEmployee, DimDate, and possibly DimDepartment if department attributes need independent tracking — otherwise I'd denormalize the department name directly onto DimEmployee to keep the star's one-join-away shape simple. DimEmployee needs full Type 2 tracking, since department and title changes are exactly what this requirement asks to historize: it carries a surrogate EmployeeKey as its clustered primary key, the natural EmployeeID as a business key, and StartDate/EndDate/IsCurrent columns. Every department or title change closes the current row (sets EndDate, IsCurrent = 0) and inserts a new row with a new surrogate key, a fresh StartDate, and IsCurrent = 1 — never an in-place UPDATE of the changing attribute. The critical design decision is that FactEmployeePerformance stores the surrogate EmployeeKey, not the natural EmployeeID, so every performance review row permanently points at the exact version of the employee's department/title that was true at review time; year-over-year reports then correctly reflect what was true then, not what's true now, which a Type 1 overwrite would silently corrupt. For indexing, DimEmployee clusters on the narrow, ever-increasing surrogate key, with a unique nonclustered index on (EmployeeID, StartDate) to support the ETL's 'which version was active on this date' lookup; the fact table gets nonclustered indexes on each dimension foreign key to support the one-join-away reporting pattern efficiently.
questions.professionalAnswer: The requirement that actually drives this whole design is 'full historical tracking of department and title changes,' so I know immediately this is a Type 2 dimension, not Type 1. I'd build FactEmployeePerformance at one-row-per-employee-per-review-period, with DimEmployee, DimDate, and department info either denormalized onto the employee dimension or split out only if it needs its own independent history. The detail I'd walk through carefully is that the fact table has to store the surrogate EmployeeKey, never the natural EmployeeID — because that surrogate is what pins a review to the exact version of the employee's department and title that was true at that moment. If we stored EmployeeID instead, a promotion six months from now would silently rewrite what last year's review 'said' about the employee's department, which is exactly the kind of quiet history corruption the client is asking us to avoid. I'd cluster the dimension on a narrow surrogate key for insert performance and add a unique index on the business key plus StartDate so the ETL can always find which version was active on a given date.
commonMistakes: Stores the natural EmployeeID in the fact table instead of the surrogate EmployeeKey, breaking Type 2 history
Uses Type 1 (overwrite) for an attribute the client explicitly wants historized
Normalizes the dimension the way an OLTP schema would, adding unnecessary joins to the star
Forgets the business-key-plus-effective-date index the ETL needs to find 'which version was active on this date'
Clusters the dimension on the natural key instead of a narrow surrogate
keyPoints: Correctly separates fact grain from dimension design
Uses a surrogate key in the fact table, not the natural key, to support Type 2 history
Implements StartDate/EndDate/IsCurrent Type 2 tracking correctly
Designs appropriate indexes for both the ETL lookup pattern and the reporting join pattern
Explains why Type 1 would be wrong for this specific requirement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct star schema design (fact grain, dimension structure)
Correctly implements SCD Type 2 with surrogate keys
Provides correct, working DDL
Sound indexing rationale for both ETL and reporting access patterns

questions.title: Designing a Federated Governance Operating Model for a 12-Business-Unit Holding Company
questions.prompt: A holding company with 12 largely autonomous business units wants one coherent data governance program without forcing every unit through a single central bottleneck. Design the federated operating model: council structure, decision rights split between center and domains, and the mechanism that keeps standards consistent without a central team reviewing everything.
questions.modelAnswer: The design has two layers with deliberately different jobs: a small central governance council that owns the things that must be consistent everywhere — the enterprise glossary's cross-cutting terms, the classification taxonomy, the minimum quality and documentation bar every data product must meet, and the platform/tooling standard — and 12 business-unit-level stewardship teams that own everything specific to their own data: their own data products, their own domain-specific glossary terms, their own stewards who actually understand that data best. Decision rights are split explicitly: the center decides what the non-negotiable minimum standards are and owns the mechanism that checks compliance against them; each business unit decides how it meets those standards and owns everything about its own data beyond that floor. The mechanism that keeps this consistent without a central bottleneck is automated, computational enforcement rather than manual central review: every business unit's data products get checked against the central minimum bar (classification present, owner assigned, quality threshold met) through platform tooling at the point of publication, not through a human at the center reviewing each one — the center's actual ongoing job becomes maintaining and evolving that automated bar, auditing a sample for drift, and running the cross-business-unit council meetings where genuinely shared questions (a term two units define differently, a new regulation affecting everyone) get resolved, rather than being in the approval path for routine work. This is deliberately the same federated computational governance pattern used in a data mesh, applied at the organizational rather than purely technical layer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this so the center only owns the things that genuinely need to be the same everywhere, and nothing else. A central council defines the non-negotiable floor — classification taxonomy, minimum documentation and quality bar, the shared parts of the glossary — and each of the 12 business units owns everything about their own data beyond that floor, including their own stewards who know that data far better than any central team ever could. The part that actually makes this scale is refusing to let 'consistent standards' turn into 'central team manually reviews everything,' because that's the bottleneck the business explicitly doesn't want. So the floor gets enforced through automated checks at the point each business unit publishes something — tagging, ownership, a basic quality gate — rather than a person at headquarters signing off on all 12 units' work one at a time. The center's real job becomes keeping that automated bar well-designed, periodically auditing a sample for drift, and convening the cross-unit conversations when something genuinely needs to be decided once for everyone, like two units defining the same term differently.
commonMistakes: Designs a fully centralized model that recreates the bottleneck the business explicitly wants to avoid
Designs a fully decentralized model with no shared standard at all, losing enterprise consistency
Doesn't specify a concrete mechanism (automated enforcement) for how the floor is checked without manual central review
Doesn't give the central council a clear, narrow, specific scope of what it actually owns
keyPoints: Designs a two-layer structure: narrow central ownership of non-negotiable standards, broad business-unit ownership of their own data
Explicitly splits decision rights between center (what the floor is) and domains (how they meet it)
Proposes automated/computational enforcement of the floor rather than manual central review
Defines the center's ongoing role as standard maintenance, auditing, and cross-unit arbitration, not approval gatekeeping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound two-layer federated structure with clear decision-rights split
Proposes a concrete mechanism avoiding a central review bottleneck
Defines a clear, appropriately narrow scope for the central council
Explains why this scales better than full centralization or full decentralization

questions.title: Designing Governance for a Data Mesh With Eight Autonomous Domain Teams
questions.prompt: Design the governance architecture for a data mesh with eight autonomous domain teams, each publishing their own data products. Cover global policy enforcement, what a data product contract must guarantee, and how discovery works across domains without a central bottleneck.
questions.modelAnswer: The design rests on three parts working together. First, a small, globally-defined policy set — classification requirements, a minimum quality SLA, mandatory ownership metadata, access control baseline — enforced computationally through the platform itself at the point any domain publishes a data product, via automated policy checks (a CI-style gate that blocks publication if the product lacks required metadata or fails a quality threshold), so the eight domains don't need a central team's manual sign-off for routine publication. Second, each data product carries an explicit contract: a documented schema with versioning commitments, a stated quality SLA (freshness, completeness thresholds), a named accountable owner, and documented access terms — the contract is what lets other domains consume the product without having to go ask the owning team what they can rely on, functioning the same way an API contract does between services. Third, discovery is centralized even though ownership and enforcement are federated: a single enterprise catalog indexes every domain's published data products regardless of which domain or platform they live on, searchable by business term and classification, so a consumer in one domain can find a relevant data product from another without needing to know it exists beforehand — this is the one piece that is deliberately centralized, because discovery genuinely benefits from a single index, while enforcement and ownership deliberately are not, because that's what preserves domain autonomy and avoids the central bottleneck.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this around a clear principle: centralize only what benefits from being centralized, and that's really just discovery. Policy and ownership stay with the domains, enforced automatically rather than through a central approval queue — every domain's platform tooling checks a small, global policy set (classification, a quality SLA, an owner on record) before anything gets published, so compliance doesn't depend on eight domains all remembering to ask permission from one team. Each data product needs an actual contract, the same way a well-designed API has one — a defined schema with versioning promises, a quality SLA, a named owner, documented access terms — because without that, a consuming domain has no way to know what they can safely build on top of without going and asking someone every time. And then discovery is the one thing I would deliberately centralize: one enterprise catalog that indexes everything across all eight domains, because that's a case where a single source of truth for 'what exists and where' genuinely helps everyone, and it doesn't cost any domain its autonomy to be searchable from one place.
commonMistakes: Centralizes policy enforcement into a manual review bottleneck instead of automating it at the platform level
Doesn't define a concrete data product contract (schema, SLA, ownership, access terms)
Centralizes ownership/enforcement along with discovery, losing the autonomy benefit mesh is meant to provide
Fails to explain why discovery specifically should be centralized while enforcement/ownership shouldn't
keyPoints: Designs automated, platform-enforced global policy checks at publication time
Defines a concrete data product contract (schema, SLA, ownership, access terms)
Centralizes discovery via a single enterprise catalog across domains
Correctly distinguishes what should be centralized (discovery) from what shouldn't (ownership/enforcement)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs automated computational governance enforcement correctly
Defines a concrete, complete data product contract
Designs centralized cross-domain discovery correctly
Explains the centralize-vs-federate reasoning clearly

questions.title: Designing a Single Pane of Glass Across Purview, Unity Catalog, and Snowflake's Native Catalogs
questions.prompt: The organization runs Databricks (Unity Catalog), Snowflake, and Power BI, each with its own native catalog, and wants one consistent search, lineage, and glossary experience across all three. Design the enterprise metadata architecture that achieves this, including where the 'system of record' for the business glossary should live.
questions.modelAnswer: Each platform's native catalog (Unity Catalog, Snowflake's account-level catalog, Power BI's semantic model layer) remains the authoritative technical system of record for its own platform's schema, permissions, and platform-specific lineage — I wouldn't try to replace or duplicate that, since each platform enforces its own access control against its own native catalog, and fighting that would both be redundant and risk permission drift between two sources of truth. The integration layer sits above all three: Purview connects to each platform via its native connectors, scanning and pulling technical metadata, classification findings, and lineage events from each into one unified data map, so a single search surfaces assets from all three platforms together and a single lineage graph can show a chain that crosses from a Databricks table into a Snowflake view into a Power BI report, something no individual platform's native catalog can show on its own since each only sees its own world. The business glossary specifically should live centrally in Purview as the single system of record, not duplicated per-platform, because a glossary term's whole value is meaning the same thing everywhere it's referenced — Purview's glossary terms get linked to the relevant technical assets across all three platforms, so 'Customer' is defined once and referenced from Databricks tables, Snowflake views, and Power BI semantic models alike, rather than three platform-specific definitions risking exactly the kind of drift that causes conflicting-numbers problems. The practical architecture is: native catalogs stay authoritative for their own platform's technical truth and access enforcement; Purview becomes the integration and business-semantics layer on top, continuously synced via scanning rather than manually maintained.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to make one tool replace all three native catalogs, because each one is also the actual enforcement point for permissions on its own platform — Unity Catalog's grants are what Databricks checks, Snowflake's RBAC is what Snowflake checks, and trying to centralize that away would just create a second source of truth that drifts from the real one. Instead, I'd treat each native catalog as staying authoritative for its own platform's technical truth, and bring Purview in above all three as the integration layer — scanning each one through its native connector so there's one search experience and one lineage graph that can actually show something crossing from Databricks into Snowflake into a Power BI report, which none of the three platforms can show on their own. The one piece I would deliberately centralize completely is the business glossary — that lives in Purview as the single system of record, with terms linked out to wherever they're actually used across all three platforms, because the entire point of a glossary term is that it means the same thing everywhere, and three separate platform-specific glossaries is just a slower way of recreating the conflicting-definitions problem governance exists to prevent.
commonMistakes: Tries to replace native catalogs' permission enforcement with a central tool instead of integrating above them
Duplicates the business glossary per platform instead of centralizing it as a single system of record
Doesn't explain the specific cross-platform value (search, lineage) that an integration layer provides over native catalogs alone
Proposes manual metadata synchronization instead of continuous scanning/integration
keyPoints: Correctly keeps each native catalog authoritative for its own platform's technical truth and access enforcement
Designs Purview (or equivalent) as an integration layer above all three via native connectors
Centralizes the business glossary as a single system of record linked across platforms
Explains the concrete cross-platform value (unified search, cross-platform lineage) this architecture provides

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the native-catalog-plus-integration-layer architecture
Correctly centralizes the business glossary with sound justification
Explains concrete cross-platform search/lineage value
Avoids proposing a redundant or conflicting second permission system

questions.title: Designing an AI Governance Review Board and Model Risk Tiering System
questions.prompt: Your organization is about to deploy its first customer-facing generative AI feature and has no model review process at all. Design an AI governance review board (composition, cadence, decision authority) and a risk-tiering framework that gives low-risk models a light review and high-risk models real scrutiny.
questions.modelAnswer: The risk-tiering framework has to exist before the board's process can be designed sensibly, because applying the same heavyweight review to every model regardless of risk is both how review boards become bottlenecks that get bypassed and how genuinely risky models get the same cursory look as a low-stakes internal tool. I'd tier by two factors: the consequence of a wrong or biased output (low: an internal productivity tool with a human always reviewing output; medium: a customer-facing tool with reversible consequences; high: anything affecting credit, employment, legal, health, or safety decisions, or any customer-facing generative AI with no human in the loop) and the degree of autonomy the model has over real decisions. Low-risk models get a lightweight self-attestation (the owning team confirms a model card and basic eval exist) with no board meeting required; medium-risk models require a documented model card, a fairness/bias evaluation, and a single designated reviewer's sign-off, asynchronously, without needing the full board; high-risk models — and this new customer-facing generative AI feature clearly qualifies — require full board review before launch. The board itself should be small and genuinely cross-functional: a model risk/compliance representative, a security representative, a representative from the business area deploying it, and a technical AI/ML lead who isn't the model's own builder, meeting on a standing cadence for scheduled reviews plus an expedited path for urgent requests, with clear decision authority to approve, approve-with-conditions, or block launch — and critically, authority that isn't advisory; if the board blocks a launch, that's binding, not a recommendation the business can route around.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build the tiering first, because without it, every review either becomes a rubber stamp for everything or a bottleneck that people start finding ways to skip — neither of which is real governance. I'd tier by the real-world consequence of the model being wrong: low risk gets a lightweight self-attestation, no board meeting needed; medium risk needs a documented model card and a bias evaluation signed off by one designated reviewer, asynchronously; and high risk — which this new customer-facing generative AI feature clearly is — goes to the full board before it ever launches. The board itself I'd keep small and genuinely cross-functional: compliance, security, someone from the actual business deploying it, and a technical lead who isn't the person who built the model, because self-review isn't real review. And I'd make sure everyone understands upfront that the board's decision is binding, not a suggestion — if it says don't launch yet, that's final, and I've seen review processes lose all credibility the first time a business team routes around a 'recommendation' that didn't have real teeth.
commonMistakes: Applies the same review intensity to every model regardless of risk, creating either a bottleneck or a rubber stamp
Doesn't define concrete tiering criteria (consequence of error, decision autonomy)
Composes the board without genuine cross-functional representation or includes the model's own builder as a reviewer
Gives the board only advisory authority instead of binding decision authority
keyPoints: Designs a concrete risk-tiering framework with clear criteria
Scales review rigor appropriately by tier (self-attestation, single-reviewer sign-off, full board)
Designs a small, genuinely cross-functional board composition
Gives the board binding, not advisory, decision authority

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound, concrete risk-tiering framework
Correctly scales review intensity by tier
Designs appropriate board composition and cadence
Establishes binding, not merely advisory, decision authority

questions.title: Designing a Complete Governance Program for an Org Whose Systems All Report Different Revenue
questions.prompt: Finance, Sales, and Product each report a different revenue number for the same quarter, and leadership has lost confidence in every number they're shown. Design, at a high level, the complete governance program you'd stand up to fix this durably: critical data elements, ownership, authoritative source designation, quality rules, catalog/glossary, and the KPIs that would prove it's working.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd sequence this rather than trying to fix everything simultaneously. Step one: identify the actual critical data element at the center of the dispute — 'revenue' isn't one thing, it's likely booked revenue, recognized revenue, and billed revenue, each legitimately different and each currently being reported by a different system as if they were interchangeable, so the first deliverable is a precise definition of each distinct concept, documented in a business glossary that leadership and all three teams agree to. Step two: assign a specific, named business owner for each distinct revenue concept — not a team, an accountable person — who is responsible for that definition staying correct and current. Step three: for each defined concept, formally designate one authoritative source system, chosen by tracing which system's data has the most direct, least-transformed path to the originating business event (an order for booked revenue, a recognition schedule for recognized revenue), documented so everyone knows which system to query for which concept. Step four: build concrete SQL-based data quality and reconciliation checks between the authoritative source and the other systems' versions of the same concept, surfacing variance for investigation rather than letting it silently resurface in a future board meeting. Step five: register all of this in the catalog — the data elements, their owners, their authoritative sources, their quality rules — so the information isn't buried in a document nobody reads. Step six: define the KPIs that prove this is working, specifically variance-between-systems trending toward zero for each defined concept, percentage of critical data elements with an active owner, and — the real test — whether leadership stops asking 'which number do I believe' in subsequent meetings. I'd present this to leadership as a 90-day sequenced plan, not a single fix, because the root problem took years to form and a credible program has to show early wins (the glossary and ownership) while the deeper reconciliation work is still in progress.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by telling leadership the blunt thing first: 'revenue' probably isn't one number that's wrong, it's three legitimately different numbers that have been presented as if they were the same thing, and the first job is separating those out, not debugging anyone's SQL. So step one is getting precise, written definitions of each real concept — likely booked, recognized, and billed revenue — into a glossary everyone signs off on. Step two, each of those gets a named accountable owner, a real person, not a team alias. Step three, for each one, I trace back to find which system sits closest to the actual originating business event and formally call that the authoritative source for that specific concept. Then I build real reconciliation checks between that authoritative source and whatever the other systems are reporting, so variance gets caught and investigated instead of surfacing as a surprise in front of leadership again. I'd present this as a sequenced plan with early visible wins — the glossary and named owners land fast — while the deeper reconciliation and tooling work continues, because a program that only promises results in six months loses the room immediately.
commonMistakes: Treats 'revenue' as one concept and tries to pick a single winning system instead of separating out the distinct legitimate definitions
Jumps to technical reconciliation/SQL fixes before establishing definitions and ownership
Assigns ownership to teams or departments instead of named accountable individuals
Doesn't define measurable KPIs that would actually prove the program worked
Presents an all-at-once fix instead of a sequenced plan with early visible wins
keyPoints: Correctly identifies that the real problem is multiple legitimate, undefined concepts sharing one ambiguous label
Sequences the program: definitions/glossary, named ownership, authoritative source designation, reconciliation checks, catalog registration, KPIs
Assigns specific named owners, not teams
Defines concrete, measurable KPIs including variance trending and ownership coverage
Presents this as a sequenced plan with early wins, appropriate for leadership communication

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the multiple-legitimate-definitions root problem
Designs a complete, correctly sequenced end-to-end program
Defines concrete, measurable success KPIs
Presents the plan in a way appropriate for leadership (sequenced, early wins)
