questions.title: Designing Consistent Classification and Access Enforcement Across Azure and AWS
questions.prompt: The same sensitive data types (customer PII) exist in both Azure Data Lake Storage and Amazon S3, governed by two completely separate native tool sets. Design how classification and access policy stay consistent across both clouds, and how compliance reporting works as a single view rather than two disconnected reports.
questions.modelAnswer: Consistency across two clouds with fundamentally different native tooling (Microsoft Purview/Entra/Azure Policy on one side, AWS Glue/Lake Formation/IAM on the other) can't come from forcing one cloud's tool to manage the other's resources natively — it has to come from a shared classification taxonomy and policy intent defined once, independently of either platform, and then translated into each platform's native enforcement mechanism. Concretely: define the classification taxonomy and the handling rules it implies (PII must be encrypted at rest, access requires a specific role, retention is X days) as policy, not as platform configuration, documented centrally; then implement that same policy twice, once as Purview classification + Azure Policy + Entra-backed RBAC on the Azure side, and once as Glue Catalog tagging + Lake Formation permissions + IAM policy on the AWS side — the implementations are necessarily platform-specific, but they're both derived from, and need to be audited against, the same source-of-truth policy definition, which prevents the two clouds' rules from silently drifting apart over time as each gets updated independently. For a single compliance view, a cross-cloud catalog/governance layer (Purview can scan AWS sources in addition to Azure natives, which is the common pattern) aggregates classification and policy-compliance status from both clouds into one reporting surface, so a compliance officer gets one dashboard showing 'is PII protected consistently' across both environments instead of needing to separately check two unrelated tools and mentally reconcile them. The architectural discipline that makes this durable is treating the policy definition as the single artifact that's version-controlled and reviewed, with each cloud's implementation treated as a derived, auditable translation of it, not as the source of truth itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to make one cloud's tool manage the other cloud's resources, because that's fighting both platforms' native security models for no real benefit. Instead, I'd define the actual policy — what PII classification means, what handling it requires, encryption, access restriction, retention — once, as a standalone, version-controlled policy document that doesn't belong to either cloud. Then that same policy gets implemented twice, once in Azure's native stack and once in AWS's, because the implementations genuinely have to be platform-specific, but both are measured against that one shared source of truth, which is what stops them from quietly drifting apart six months later when someone updates one side and not the other. For reporting, I'd bring in a catalog layer that can actually scan both environments — Purview can reach into AWS sources, which is the pattern I'd use — so compliance sees one dashboard instead of stitching together two separate tools' reports by hand. The real architectural discipline here isn't the tooling, it's treating the policy itself, not either cloud's configuration, as the thing that's actually authoritative.
commonMistakes: Tries to force one cloud's native tool to directly manage the other cloud's resources
Defines policy separately and natively per-cloud with no shared source of truth, allowing drift
Proposes maintaining two completely separate compliance reports instead of a unified cross-cloud view
Doesn't address how policy updates stay synchronized across both implementations over time
keyPoints: Defines a platform-independent policy as the single source of truth
Implements that policy natively and appropriately on each cloud without cross-cloud tool dependency
Designs a cross-cloud catalog/reporting layer for a unified compliance view
Addresses how drift is prevented between the two platform-specific implementations over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs policy-as-shared-source-of-truth with platform-specific implementation
Designs a sound cross-cloud reporting/catalog layer
Addresses drift prevention between the two implementations
Avoids proposing an unworkable single-tool-manages-both-clouds design

questions.title: Designing the Purview Collection and Domain Hierarchy for a 40-Subsidiary Conglomerate
questions.prompt: A 40-subsidiary conglomerate wants one Purview account serving all of them without any single subsidiary's scanning or access needs becoming a bottleneck for the others. Design the collection/domain hierarchy, scan automation approach, and the mechanism that keeps one Purview account from becoming an operational chokepoint.
questions.modelAnswer: A single flat collection with 40 subsidiaries' sources dumped into it would make role assignment and scan management unmanageable and would force every permission decision through whoever administers the root. The design instead uses Purview's collection hierarchy to mirror the organizational structure: a root collection owned by the central governance team, with one child collection per subsidiary (or per logical grouping of smaller subsidiaries sharing similar needs), and critically, collection-level role assignment delegated down — each subsidiary's own data stewards get Data Curator/Reader roles scoped only to their own collection, so they can register sources, manage classifications, and curate their own assets without needing the central team to act on their behalf for routine work, and without being able to see or touch other subsidiaries' collections. Scan automation follows the same delegation principle: each subsidiary's collection has its own scan configurations and schedules, ideally triggered through infrastructure-as-code or a self-service template the subsidiary's own data engineering team can use to register new sources against a pre-approved scan rule set, rather than requiring the central team to manually configure every new source across 40 organizations. The mechanism that prevents the central Purview account from becoming a chokepoint is this combination of delegated collection-scoped permissions and self-service scan configuration within guardrails — the central team's actual job becomes maintaining the collection structure itself, the shared classification/scan rule set standards, and handling only genuinely cross-subsidiary concerns (a shared vendor, an enterprise-wide regulation), not being in the operational path for each subsidiary's day-to-day scanning and curation.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design principle I'd lead with is delegation, because a single team can't realistically be the operational bottleneck for 40 subsidiaries without either becoming a massive team or becoming the thing that makes the whole program fail to scale. So I mirror the org structure in Purview's collection hierarchy — a root collection the central team owns, one child collection per subsidiary — and I push real role assignment down to that level, so each subsidiary's own stewards can curate their own assets and register their own sources without needing someone centrally to do it for them, and without seeing anyone else's collection. Scanning follows the same logic: I'd set up a self-service template within pre-approved guardrails so each subsidiary's own team can onboard a new source against a known-good scan rule set, rather than filing a ticket to a central team every time. What's left for the central team is the stuff that actually needs to be central — maintaining the shared classification standards, handling the rare cross-subsidiary issue — and deliberately nothing else, because anything else becomes the bottleneck this design is supposed to avoid.
commonMistakes: Designs a flat collection structure or centralizes all role assignment, recreating the bottleneck
Doesn't delegate collection-scoped permissions down to each subsidiary's own stewards
Requires central-team manual configuration for every new source instead of self-service within guardrails
Doesn't clearly define what should remain genuinely central versus delegated
keyPoints: Designs a collection hierarchy mirroring the organizational structure
Delegates collection-scoped role assignment to each subsidiary's own stewards
Designs self-service scan configuration within central guardrails
Clearly scopes the central team's remaining role to standards maintenance and genuinely cross-cutting issues

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correct, scalable collection hierarchy
Correctly delegates role assignment and curation to subsidiaries
Designs sound self-service scan automation within guardrails
Clearly scopes the central team's remaining responsibilities

questions.title: Designing Unity Catalog Metastore Topology for Regional Data Residency
questions.prompt: A global company using Databricks has data residency requirements in the EU, US, and APAC — data in each region legally cannot leave it. Design the Unity Catalog metastore topology that satisfies this, including catalog naming conventions and how (or whether) any cross-region governed access is handled.
questions.modelAnswer: Given that a metastore is a regional construct and its metadata (and, depending on managed storage configuration, the data itself) is anchored to the region it's created in, the only design that genuinely satisfies hard data residency requirements is one metastore per region — EU, US, APAC — each with its own managed storage location physically within that region's boundary, rather than a single global metastore that would violate residency the moment it spans regions. Within each regional metastore, I'd apply a consistent catalog naming convention across all three (e.g., prod_sales, prod_finance as catalog names repeated identically in each region's metastore) so that despite being physically separate metastores, the experience for someone working across regions feels uniform — the same catalog name means the same thing conceptually in every region, even though it's technically a distinct object in each metastore with its own data. Cross-region governed access is the harder design question: Unity Catalog's Delta Sharing capability can share specific tables across metastores (and even across organizations) without physically moving or replicating the underlying data wholesale, so if a genuine business need exists for an aggregated, non-resident-restricted view (like a global sales summary that doesn't itself contain residency-restricted row-level detail), Delta Sharing lets that specific aggregated table be shared from each region into a central reporting metastore deliberately and auditably, rather than the regional metastores being invisibly interconnected by default. The discipline that matters architecturally: residency compliance comes from the metastores being genuinely separate by default, with any cross-region data flow being an explicit, documented, auditable exception via Delta Sharing, never an implicit capability of the platform.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given hard residency requirements, I'm not going to recommend anything other than metastore-per-region here — EU, US, APAC each get their own metastore with managed storage that's physically within that region, because that's the only way to guarantee data doesn't technically cross a boundary it's not allowed to cross. What I do keep consistent across all three is the catalog naming convention — the same catalog names repeated in each region's metastore — so working across regions feels uniform even though under the hood these are genuinely separate objects in separate metastores. The harder question is what happens when the business legitimately needs something that spans regions, like a global aggregate report. For that, I'd use Delta Sharing to deliberately and auditably share specific, already-aggregated tables from each regional metastore into a central reporting metastore — not because the regions are secretly connected, but because that one specific need was explicitly designed for and documented, which is a very different thing from the platform just allowing cross-region access by default.
commonMistakes: Proposes a single global metastore for simplicity, violating residency requirements
Doesn't propose a consistent naming convention across regional metastores, creating a confusing cross-region experience
Doesn't address the legitimate cross-region reporting need at all, or addresses it by weakening residency boundaries
Proposes an implicit or default cross-region data flow instead of an explicit, auditable exception via Delta Sharing
keyPoints: Correctly designs metastore-per-region as the only compliant topology
Proposes a consistent catalog naming convention across regions
Uses Delta Sharing for deliberate, auditable cross-region sharing of non-restricted aggregated data
Frames cross-region access as an explicit exception, never an implicit platform default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs metastore-per-region topology
Proposes a sound cross-region naming convention
Correctly uses Delta Sharing for deliberate cross-region access
Frames residency compliance as the default, not an afterthought

questions.title: Designing Governance Consistency Across 15 Snowflake Accounts in One Organization
questions.prompt: A Snowflake Organization spans 15 accounts (by region and business unit), and RBAC, masking policies, and tagging are currently configured by hand in each one, drifting out of sync. Design how governance stays consistent across all 15 without manual, per-account configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: Fifteen accounts configured by hand will drift by definition — the fix isn't more discipline, it's removing the manual step entirely through governance-as-code. I'd define the shared governance objects — role hierarchy templates, masking policy definitions, tag definitions and their allowed values, row access policy templates — as version-controlled SQL/Terraform-style definitions in a single repository, treated as the actual source of truth rather than whatever happens to exist in any given account. A deployment pipeline then applies that same definition set to every account (or to every account matching a given profile, since regional accounts may need region-specific values like which role maps to which data residency boundary) via Snowflake's SQL execution or the Terraform provider for Snowflake, so a change to a masking policy's logic is authored once and deployed consistently everywhere, rather than being manually re-created 15 times with 15 chances to introduce a subtle difference. For organization-wide reporting, Snowflake's ACCOUNT_USAGE and ORGANIZATION_USAGE views (available to an org-level role) let a central governance team query grant and policy state across all 15 accounts from one place, which both verifies the deployment pipeline actually kept everything in sync and gives a single audit answer instead of 15 separate ones. The discipline that makes this durable is the same as any infrastructure-as-code pattern: nobody manually edits an individual account's RBAC or masking policy directly anymore — every change goes through the pipeline, so the repository and the deployed reality can't drift apart by someone taking a shortcut in one account.
questions.professionalAnswer: Fifteen hand-configured accounts are going to drift, that's not really in question — so my fix is removing hand-configuration as an option at all. I'd put the actual governance definitions — roles, masking policies, tag definitions and allowed values — into version-controlled code, using something like the Terraform provider for Snowflake, and treat that repository as the real source of truth, not whatever's currently sitting in any one account. A pipeline deploys that same definition set across all 15 accounts, with room for account-specific values where genuinely needed, like region-specific residency mappings. For visibility, I'd use the organization-level usage views so a central team can query grant and policy state across every account from one place instead of logging into 15 consoles to check whether they still match. And the real discipline isn't just setting this up once — it's making sure nobody goes around the pipeline and hand-edits an individual account afterward, because that's exactly how the drift started in the first place.
commonMistakes: Proposes more manual process/documentation discipline instead of removing manual configuration via governance-as-code
Doesn't propose a concrete deployment mechanism (Terraform/pipeline) for applying definitions across all 15 accounts
Doesn't address organization-level visibility/auditing across accounts
Doesn't address the ongoing discipline needed to prevent someone from manually editing an individual account post-rollout
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses manual per-account configuration as the root cause of drift
Designs a governance-as-code approach with a version-controlled source of truth
Proposes a concrete deployment mechanism across all 15 accounts
Designs organization-level visibility/auditing and ongoing discipline to prevent drift recurrence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses manual configuration as the root cause
Designs a sound governance-as-code approach with a real source of truth
Proposes a concrete cross-account deployment mechanism
Designs organization-level visibility and drift-prevention discipline

questions.title: Designing the Workspace and Deployment Pipeline Topology for 200 Power BI Workspaces
questions.prompt: The organization has grown to roughly 200 Power BI workspaces with no consistent naming, no clear dev/test/prod separation, and uncertainty about which datasets are actually authoritative. Design the workspace structure, deployment pipeline topology, and certification governance that would bring order to this at scale.
questions.modelAnswer: At 200 workspaces, ad hoc organization has already failed, so the design needs an enforced naming and structural convention, not just a recommended one. I'd require every workspace name to encode its domain and environment (e.g., SALES-PROD, SALES-TEST, SALES-DEV), enforced through a workspace creation process (ideally a self-service request that provisions the full dev/test/prod trio together rather than letting teams create a single workspace and never set up the other stages) so the convention isn't optional. Each domain's trio uses Power BI deployment pipelines to move content from dev through test into production in a controlled, auditable sequence, rather than teams manually publishing directly to whatever workspace they consider 'production' — this is what actually prevents an untested change from landing directly in front of business users. Certification governance is centralized regardless of how distributed workspace ownership is: certification permission is restricted via tenant settings to a specific governance group, and a dataset only earns certified status after passing a defined review (not simply because a team wants their dataset to look authoritative), with a visible, searchable registry of which datasets are certified so 'which number do I trust' has one discoverable answer instead of 200 workspaces' worth of guessing. For discoverability and governance oversight at this scale, I'd also require every workspace to be assigned to a Fabric/Power BI domain matching the naming convention, so admin-level reporting (usage metrics, audit logs) can be sliced by domain rather than needing to reason about 200 individual workspaces one at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: At 200 workspaces, I don't think a 'recommended' naming convention is going to hold — it needs to be enforced at creation time, not suggested afterward. So I'd set up a self-service provisioning process that creates a domain's dev, test, and prod workspaces together as a named trio, with the environment baked into the name, so there's no ambiguity about which one is actually production. Promotion between them goes through Power BI deployment pipelines, not someone manually publishing to whatever they've decided is prod this week, because that pipeline step is what actually stops an untested change from landing in front of business users. For certification, I'd lock that permission down to a specific governance group via tenant settings regardless of how many workspaces exist, and keep one visible, searchable registry of what's actually certified, because the real problem at 200 workspaces isn't just disorganization, it's that nobody can tell which of several similar-looking datasets is the one to trust. And I'd require every workspace to carry a domain assignment that matches its name, so admin reporting can actually be sliced sensibly instead of being 200 unrelated data points.
commonMistakes: Proposes a naming convention as a guideline/recommendation rather than an enforced creation-time requirement
Doesn't design dev/test/prod as a provisioned trio with deployment pipelines between them
Leaves certification permission unrestricted or doesn't centralize it despite distributed workspace ownership
Doesn't address discoverability of which datasets are actually certified at this scale
keyPoints: Designs an enforced, creation-time naming/structure convention
Designs a dev/test/prod trio provisioning process using deployment pipelines
Centralizes certification permission via tenant settings regardless of workspace count
Designs domain assignment and a visible certified-dataset registry for discoverability at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs an enforced naming/structure convention
Designs a sound dev/test/prod deployment pipeline topology
Correctly centralizes certification governance
Addresses discoverability and domain-based oversight at scale

questions.title: Using Architecture Decision Records to Prevent a Platform Choice From Being Re-Litigated
questions.prompt: The decision to centralize scanning and classification in Purview rather than relying on each platform's native catalog keeps getting re-argued every quarter by whoever is newest to the governance team. Design what a governance ADR template should capture for a decision like this, and explain why that documentation discipline is an architectural control, not just administrative overhead.
questions.modelAnswer: A governance ADR needs to capture more than the decision itself, because the recurring re-litigation almost always happens because the context that justified the decision was never written down, so each new person is reasoning from scratch with incomplete information rather than evaluating whether anything has actually changed. The template should include: the specific context and constraints at the time (what platforms existed, what the alternatives genuinely were, what tradeoffs were explicitly weighed — e.g., 'per-platform native catalogs were considered and rejected because they can't provide unified cross-platform search or lineage, which was a stated requirement'); the decision itself, stated unambiguously; the consequences accepted as a result (what we deliberately gave up — e.g., 'this adds Purview as a dependency and requires maintaining connector configurations per platform'); and a status/review field distinguishing a still-valid decision from one that's been superseded, with the date and reasoning for any supersession. This functions as an actual architectural control, not paperwork, because it converts 'why do we do it this way' from a question only the original decision-makers can answer from memory (and memory degrades and people leave) into a durable artifact anyone can check — and specifically, it changes the burden of proof: re-opening a documented decision now requires showing what's materially changed since the ADR was written, rather than the decision needing to be re-defended from zero by whoever happens to be in the room this quarter. Without it, the architecture is only as stable as the turnover rate of the people who remember why it was built that way.
questions.professionalAnswer: The reason this keeps getting re-argued is almost certainly that nobody wrote down why it was decided in the first place, so every new person reasonably asks the question again, and without a record, the only answer available is whatever the most senior person in the room remembers, which degrades every time someone leaves. So the ADR template I'd use captures the real context at decision time — what alternatives were actually considered and specifically why they were rejected, not just 'we picked Purview' — plus the consequences we knowingly accepted by choosing this path, and a status field that says whether this is still the active decision or has been formally superseded, with a date and reason if so. The architectural value here isn't the document itself, it's what it changes about future conversations: instead of 'let's re-debate this from scratch,' the question becomes 'has anything actually changed since this was decided,' which is a much higher and more productive bar than re-litigating a decision every time someone new joins the team.
commonMistakes: Designs a template that only records the decision, not the context, alternatives considered, and accepted consequences
Treats the ADR as a one-time document rather than something with a status field for supersession over time
Doesn't explain the actual mechanism by which an ADR prevents re-litigation (shifting the burden of proof)
Frames this as purely administrative rather than explaining its architectural function
keyPoints: Designs a complete ADR template: context, alternatives considered and rejected, decision, accepted consequences, status/supersession
Explains why undocumented decisions degrade as institutional memory turns over
Explains the specific mechanism by which an ADR prevents re-litigation (shifts burden of proof to 'what's changed')
Frames documentation discipline as an architectural control, not administrative overhead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a complete, correctly structured ADR template
Explains why undocumented decisions degrade over time
Explains the specific mechanism preventing re-litigation
Frames this correctly as an architectural, not administrative, control

questions.title: Designing End-to-End Lineage From Raw Source Data Through a Deployed Model's Predictions
questions.prompt: Design the lineage architecture spanning traditional data lineage (raw source to feature store) and AI-specific lineage (feature store to training run to model version to deployed endpoint to a specific prediction). Explain what breaks, concretely, if any one link in that chain isn't captured.
questions.modelAnswer: The chain has two halves that need different capture mechanisms stitched together at one connecting point. The data-lineage half (raw source tables through transformation pipelines to a feature store) is well-served by standard data catalog/lineage tooling that already tracks column-to-column transformation through ETL/ELT pipelines, ending at the feature store as a registered, versioned asset. The AI-specific half has to pick up from there: the training run itself must record exactly which feature store snapshot/version it consumed (not just 'the feature store,' but the specific point-in-time version), along with the code version and hyperparameters, producing a model version that's registered with that training run's identity attached; the model version then gets deployed to a specific serving endpoint, and that deployment event itself needs to be recorded (which model version is live, from which date); finally, at inference time, each prediction response should carry (at minimum, loggable) a reference to which model version and endpoint produced it, so a specific prediction can be traced backward through deployment, to model version, to training run, to feature snapshot, to original source data. Concretely, if the training-run-to-feature-snapshot link is missing, you can say a model exists and what it predicted, but not what data actually shaped its behavior — which defeats any audit asking 'was this trained on data that should have been excluded.' If the deployment-event link is missing, you can't reliably answer 'which model version was live when this specific customer got this specific prediction,' which is often the exact question an adverse-decision dispute or regulatory inquiry asks first. The architecture has to treat this as one continuous chain with explicit hand-off points, rather than two separate lineage systems that happen to sit next to each other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this as two halves stitched together at one deliberate hand-off point, because trying to force one tool to natively understand both data lineage and AI-specific lineage usually doesn't work well in practice. Standard catalog/lineage tooling handles the data side fine — raw source through transformations to a feature store, as a versioned asset. From there, the AI-specific chain has to explicitly record: which exact feature store snapshot a training run consumed, not just 'the feature store' generically; the resulting model version, tied back to that training run; which endpoint that model version got deployed to, and when; and ideally, enough logging at inference time to trace a specific prediction back to the model version that produced it. If any one of those links is missing, the practical damage is concrete, not abstract — miss the training-to-snapshot link and you can't answer an audit asking what data actually trained this model; miss the deployment-event link and you can't answer the much more common question, 'which version of the model was live when this specific customer got this specific decision,' which is usually the first thing an actual dispute or regulatory inquiry asks.
commonMistakes: Treats data lineage and AI lineage as one undifferentiated system instead of designing the explicit hand-off point
Doesn't specify that training runs must reference a specific feature snapshot version, not just 'the feature store' generically
Omits the deployment event (which model version is live, and when) from the chain
Describes the chain abstractly without identifying the concrete audit question that fails if a specific link is missing
keyPoints: Designs the data-lineage half and AI-lineage half with an explicit connecting hand-off point
Specifies training-run-to-feature-snapshot versioning as a required link
Specifies the deployment event (model version, endpoint, date) as a required link
Gives concrete, realistic examples of what fails if a specific link is missing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correct, complete end-to-end lineage chain with a clear hand-off point
Correctly specifies training-run-to-feature-snapshot versioning
Correctly specifies the deployment event as a required link
Gives concrete, realistic consequences of missing links

questions.title: Designing a Policy-as-Code Pipeline That Enforces Governance Before Production
questions.prompt: Rather than scanning for ungoverned data assets after the fact and remediating them, design a CI/CD-integrated policy-as-code architecture that blocks a new data asset's deployment if it lacks required classification and ownership metadata, before it ever reaches production.
questions.modelAnswer: The architectural shift is moving the governance check from a scheduled scan that discovers problems after deployment to a gate embedded directly in the deployment pipeline that evaluates before deployment completes, which changes the failure mode from 'we eventually notice this is ungoverned' to 'this never becomes ungoverned in the first place.' Concretely: every new data asset's definition (a table DDL, a dataset registration manifest, an infrastructure-as-code template provisioning storage) should carry its governance metadata — classification, owner, retention policy — as a required, structured part of that same definition, not as a separate manual step performed afterward. A policy engine (something like Open Policy Agent, or a platform-native equivalent such as Azure Policy for infrastructure-level resources) evaluates that metadata against the organization's required-fields policy as a step in the CI/CD pipeline, before the apply/deploy step runs — failing the build and blocking deployment if required metadata is missing or invalid, the same way a failing unit test blocks a code deployment today. This requires the policy rules themselves to be version-controlled code, reviewed through the same pull-request process as any other infrastructure change, so updates to governance requirements go through the same scrutiny as the systems they govern. The after-the-fact scanning approach still has a role — as a safety net catching anything that was deployed through a path outside the governed pipeline, or catching drift in metadata that was valid at deployment time but has since gone stale — but it's a backstop, not the primary enforcement mechanism, which is the structural change from detect-and-remediate to prevent-by-design.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real shift I'd design for is moving the check earlier — from 'a scan finds this was ungoverned, eventually' to 'this literally cannot deploy without the required metadata.' So I'd make classification, ownership, and retention required fields in whatever already defines the asset — a table DDL, a dataset manifest, an infrastructure template — rather than a separate step someone has to remember to do after the fact. Then a policy engine, run as a step in the CI/CD pipeline before deployment actually happens, checks that metadata the same way a failing test blocks a bad code deploy today — if it's missing or invalid, the deployment just doesn't go through. And the policy rules themselves need to live in version control and go through the same review process as any other change, because otherwise the rules drift out of sync with reality just as easily as the assets they're supposed to govern. I'd keep the after-the-fact scanning running too, but as a safety net for things that snuck in through some other path, not as the main defense — the main defense is that the ungoverned state can't happen in the first place.
commonMistakes: Proposes only after-the-fact scanning/remediation rather than a true pre-deployment gate
Doesn't require governance metadata as a structured, required part of the asset's own definition
Doesn't version-control the policy rules themselves or subject them to review
Discards after-the-fact scanning entirely instead of keeping it as a backstop for out-of-band deployments
keyPoints: Designs a true pre-deployment policy gate embedded in CI/CD, not after-the-fact scanning
Requires governance metadata as a structured, required part of the asset's own definition
Version-controls and reviews the policy rules themselves
Retains after-the-fact scanning as a backstop, not the primary mechanism

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correct pre-deployment policy-as-code gate
Correctly requires governance metadata as part of the asset definition
Addresses version control/review of the policy rules themselves
Correctly positions after-the-fact scanning as a backstop, not the primary mechanism

questions.title: Prioritizing a Backlog of Competing Dashboard Requests
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had a large backlog of dashboard and report requests from multiple departments, all claiming urgency. How did you build a prioritization framework and communicate it back to stakeholders?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should quantify the backlog problem — number of open requests, number of competing departments, and why 'everything is urgent' had become the default. It should describe a concrete prioritization framework rather than ad hoc judgment calls: scoring requests against criteria like business impact, number of downstream decisions affected, cost of delay, and build effort, and making that framework visible to requesters rather than opaque. It should show how the framework was communicated back to stakeholders whose requests ranked lower — specifically how the candidate avoided just disappointing people silently, by explaining the reasoning and giving a realistic timeline. Strong answers mention a lightweight intake and triage process (a backlog board, a regular grooming cadence) so prioritization becomes repeatable rather than a one-time exercise, and close with a measurable outcome: reduced average time-to-delivery, fewer 'why hasn't my request been touched' escalations, or higher stakeholder satisfaction with transparency even when their request wasn't first in line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I inherited a backlog of 47 open dashboard requests across six departments, each department insisting theirs was the most urgent, with no shared criteria for sequencing any of it. I built a simple scoring model with four weighted factors — number of people who'd use it regularly, whether it supported a recurring decision versus a one-off curiosity, estimated build effort, and cost of continuing to delay it — and scored every open request against it in a spreadsheet I made visible to all six department leads, not just my own team. I ran a 30-minute session with each lead to walk through how their specific requests scored and why, which let me say 'your request is real and matters, here's exactly where it lands and why' instead of a vague 'we'll get to it.' Two leads pushed back hard on their ranking, and in one case they were right — I'd underweighted a compliance-driven request from Legal that had a hard regulatory deadline I hadn't accounted for, so I added a deadline-override factor to the model. We moved to a visible Kanban board with a biweekly grooming session so this became routine instead of a one-time fire drill. Average time from request to delivery dropped from eleven weeks to under four, and escalations to my manager about 'my request is stuck' dropped to nearly zero because people could see exactly where they stood and why.
commonMistakes: No concrete scoring criteria, just 'we prioritized based on urgency'
Keeping the prioritization logic opaque instead of sharing it with requesters
Not addressing how deprioritized stakeholders were communicated with
Treating the first prioritization pass as final instead of being open to correction
No repeatable process established, just a one-time cleanup
No measurable improvement in delivery time or stakeholder satisfaction
keyPoints: Quantifies the backlog and the competing-urgency problem
Introduces a concrete, weighted prioritization framework
Makes the framework and resulting rankings visible to stakeholders
Shows willingness to revise the framework when a legitimate gap is found
Establishes a repeatable intake/grooming process, not a one-time fix
Gives a measurable improvement in delivery time or escalation volume

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Concreteness of the prioritization framework
Transparency with stakeholders about rankings and reasoning
Willingness to revise the framework when challenged
Repeatability of the process going forward
Measurable outcome

questions.title: Leading an Organization's First Enterprise Data Governance Program From Zero
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you led the launch of an organization's very first formal data governance program. How did you decide what to tackle first, and how did you get buy-in before you had any track record to point to?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to start everywhere at once and instead describes a deliberately narrow first scope — one or two critical data elements with visible, already-felt pain, rather than an enterprise-wide rollout on day one, since a first governance program with no track record needs a believable early win more than it needs comprehensive coverage. It should explain how buy-in was earned without prior credibility: typically by anchoring the pitch to a cost or risk the organization already recognized (a specific incident, a specific executive complaint about conflicting numbers) rather than an abstract governance pitch, and by securing one or two visible executive sponsors who would publicly back the first phase rather than trying to win over the whole organization simultaneously. It should describe concrete first steps (identifying the first critical data elements, assigning the first real stewards, establishing the first authoritative source) and close with how that early, narrow win was used to earn the mandate for broader rollout — the sequencing itself, not just the content, is the behavioral competency being assessed here.
questions.professionalAnswer: I didn't try to launch an enterprise-wide program on day one, because nothing earns skepticism faster than a brand-new governance function showing up with a broad mandate and zero track record. I picked one very specific, already-painful problem — in my case, three systems disagreeing on 'active customer count' in a way that had already embarrassed someone in an executive meeting — and scoped the first 90 days entirely around fixing that one thing visibly: naming the real owner, agreeing on one definition, designating one authoritative source. I got one executive sponsor who'd personally been burned by the conflicting numbers to publicly back that narrow effort, rather than trying to get buy-in from everyone simultaneously before I'd shipped anything. Once that specific problem was visibly fixed and that sponsor was willing to say so in a leadership meeting, I had something concrete to point to when I asked for the mandate to expand the program to a second, then a third critical data element — the credibility came from the win, not from the pitch.
commonMistakes: Describes launching a broad, enterprise-wide program immediately with no narrow first scope
Pitches governance abstractly instead of anchoring to a specific, already-recognized pain point
Doesn't secure a concrete executive sponsor for the first phase
Doesn't describe how an early win was used to earn the mandate for subsequent expansion
keyPoints: Describes a deliberately narrow, high-pain first scope rather than a broad launch
Anchors the buy-in pitch to a specific, already-recognized problem rather than abstract governance value
Secures a concrete executive sponsor for the first phase
Uses the early win's credibility to earn the mandate for subsequent program expansion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a sound, narrow first-phase scope
Anchors buy-in to a specific, recognized problem
Secures and leverages a concrete executive sponsor
Shows how the early win earned the mandate for expansion

questions.title: Standing Up an AI Governance Review Board From Scratch
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to design and launch a review process for approving AI/ML models before production deployment, when no such process existed. Who did you bring to the table, and how did you handle the first model that failed review?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes concrete composition decisions — who specifically was brought onto the review board and why that mix mattered (compliance, security, the business owner, an independent technical reviewer who wasn't the model's own builder) — rather than a vague 'we formed a committee.' It should address the real friction point directly: how the candidate handled the very first model that failed review, since that moment sets the precedent for whether the board has real teeth or becomes a rubber stamp the first time it's inconvenient. A strong answer shows the candidate held the line on that first failure despite pressure (a launch deadline, a frustrated product team) rather than quietly waiving the requirement to avoid conflict, and explains how that decision was communicated — specifically, framing the rejection constructively (what needs to change, not just 'no') so the team doesn't conclude the board exists to say no rather than to help ship responsibly. It should close with how that first case shaped the board's credibility and process going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I pulled together a small group deliberately — someone from compliance, someone from security, the product owner whose team actually needed the model shipped, and a technical reviewer from a different team than the one that built the model, specifically because I didn't want the model's own author also being the person who approved it. The real test came almost immediately: the first model through the new process was a churn-prediction model that failed because its training data had a known gap for a specific customer segment, and the team pushing it had a launch date already announced externally. I held the line and didn't wave it through, which was uncomfortable, but I made sure the rejection came with exactly what needed to change and a realistic path to get there, not just a 'no' — we worked with them on a mitigation (flagging predictions for that segment as lower-confidence rather than blocking launch entirely) that let them hit a revised date while actually fixing the real gap. That case became the thing I pointed to afterward whenever someone asked whether this board was serious — because it had already said no once, under real pressure, and the model that eventually shipped was genuinely better for it.
commonMistakes: Describes a vague committee with no specific, deliberate composition rationale
Waives or softens the first rejection under deadline pressure, undermining the board's credibility from day one
Communicates the rejection as a bare 'no' without a constructive path forward
Doesn't connect the first difficult case to how it shaped the board's ongoing credibility
keyPoints: Describes deliberate, justified board composition, including independent technical review
Holds the line on the first real rejection despite real business pressure
Communicates the rejection constructively, with a concrete path forward
Connects that first case to the board's lasting credibility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes deliberate, well-justified board composition
Holds the line on the first rejection despite pressure
Communicates the rejection constructively with a path forward
Connects the case to the board's ongoing credibility

questions.title: Leading a Team Through a Data Quality Incident That Reached the Executive Team
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a data quality issue became serious enough to reach executive leadership, and you had to both manage the incident and support your team through it. What did you do in the first 24 hours, and how did you handle the postmortem?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates two distinct jobs the candidate had to do simultaneously — managing the actual incident and protecting/leading the team working it — and describes both concretely. For the first 24 hours: establishing scope and impact quickly (what data, how many downstream reports/decisions were affected, is it still actively wrong or already corrected), communicating a factual status to executives early even before a root cause was known, rather than going silent until everything was solved, and shielding the team from direct executive pressure while they worked so they could focus. For the postmortem, a strong answer describes a genuinely blameless process focused on process and system gaps rather than individual fault, with specific, assigned, and later-verified-as-completed action items — not just a one-time apology document — and shows how the candidate handled their own accountability to leadership (owning the outcome at their level) while protecting individual team members from being scapegoated for a systemic gap.
questions.professionalAnswer: In the first few hours, my focus was scope, not blame — what data was actually wrong, how far downstream had it traveled, which decisions had already been made on bad numbers, and I gave leadership a factual update on exactly that within a couple of hours, even though I didn't have a root cause yet, because going quiet while people are anxious is worse than saying 'here's what we know, here's what we're still finding out.' I deliberately took the executive-facing updates off my team's plate so they could stay focused on actually fixing it instead of also managing upward pressure. The postmortem I ran was explicitly blameless — we talked about what allowed this to happen structurally, not who made the mistake, because the person who touched the pipeline wasn't the real root cause, a missing validation step was. I personally owned the outcome in front of leadership rather than letting it land on whoever happened to be on call, and we walked away with specific action items with named owners and dates, which I followed up on at 30 and 60 days to confirm they'd actually been done, not just written down and forgotten.
commonMistakes: Focuses only on the technical fix without addressing team support or executive communication
Goes silent with executives until a full root cause is known instead of giving early factual updates
Runs a blame-oriented postmortem instead of a blameless, systems-focused one
Doesn't follow up to verify postmortem action items were actually completed
Lets an individual team member absorb blame for a systemic/process gap
keyPoints: Describes concrete first-24-hour actions: scoping impact and giving early factual executive updates
Shields the team from direct pressure while they work the incident
Runs a genuinely blameless postmortem focused on process/system gaps
Assigns specific, dated action items and follows up to confirm completion
Personally owns the outcome with leadership rather than letting it fall on an individual

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes concrete, sound first-24-hour incident actions
Shows genuine team protection/leadership during the incident
Runs a genuinely blameless, systems-focused postmortem
Assigns and verifies concrete follow-up action items

questions.title: Convincing Skeptical Leadership to Adopt a Federated Governance Model
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to convince leadership to move away from a centralized governance approach they were comfortable with, toward a federated model, when they were skeptical it would just create inconsistency. How did you make the case?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer takes leadership's underlying fear seriously rather than dismissing it — the worry that federation means inconsistency is legitimate, since a badly-federated model genuinely does produce exactly that, so the candidate needs to show they addressed the real concern rather than just arguing for autonomy in the abstract. It should describe the actual evidence used to make the case: likely a concrete, felt cost of the existing centralized bottleneck (specific delays, a backlog, teams routing around the central team because it couldn't keep up) paired with a specific design answer to the consistency worry — the automated/computational enforcement mechanism that keeps a minimum standard consistent even without central manual review. A strong answer describes a staged or piloted rollout rather than asking leadership to commit to the new model wholesale on faith, and closes with how the pilot's results (or a comparable proof point) were used to earn broader adoption, showing the persuasion was evidence-based and incremental rather than a single big pitch.
questions.professionalAnswer: I didn't try to argue them out of their worry, because it was a legitimate one — federation done badly really does produce inconsistency, so dismissing that concern would have just made me look like I hadn't thought it through. Instead I led with the cost of staying centralized that they were already feeling: a six-week backlog for anything needing central governance review, and I had examples of teams starting to quietly route around the central team because it couldn't keep up, which is actually worse for consistency than a well-designed federated model would be. Then I addressed their actual fear directly with a specific design, not a promise: an automated minimum-standard check built into the platform that every domain's output had to pass regardless of who owned it, so consistency didn't depend on a central team manually reviewing everything, it was enforced structurally. I asked for a pilot with two domains rather than a full commitment, and when the pilot showed those two domains moving faster while still passing the same consistency checks as before, that result — not my original pitch — is what actually got the broader rollout approved.
commonMistakes: Dismisses leadership's consistency concern instead of taking it seriously and addressing it directly
Argues for federation on philosophical/autonomy grounds without a concrete design answer to the consistency risk
Asks for full commitment upfront instead of proposing a staged or piloted rollout
Doesn't use the pilot's actual results to drive the broader decision
keyPoints: Takes the consistency concern seriously rather than dismissing it
Presents a concrete felt cost of the status quo as part of the case
Addresses the consistency worry with a specific design (automated enforcement), not just reassurance
Proposes and uses a piloted rollout to earn broader adoption based on evidence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Takes the underlying consistency concern seriously and addresses it directly
Presents a concrete cost of the status quo
Proposes a specific structural answer to the consistency risk
Uses a piloted/staged approach with real results to drive adoption

questions.title: Resolving an Ownership Dispute Between Two Business Units Over the Same Data
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time two business units each claimed ownership (or each disclaimed ownership) of the same critical data element, and you had to resolve it. What framework did you use, and how did you keep both sides engaged afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific, non-arbitrary framework used to resolve the dispute rather than simply picking a side or escalating it upward to be decided by someone else's authority — a reasonable approach is tracing which unit is actually closest to the originating business event or process that creates the data, since ownership is generally best assigned to whoever can most directly influence and is most affected by the data's quality, not whoever uses it most or shouts loudest. It should address the harder case explicitly: what happens when both units disclaim ownership (each saying it's not really their job) rather than fight over it, which requires a different intervention — making the cost of no ownership visible and concrete, since an unowned critical data element has real, demonstrable consequences that neither unit wants attributed to their inaction. A strong answer describes how the losing (or newly-assigned) side was kept genuinely engaged afterward rather than feeling overruled — for example, giving them a defined consulted role even though they're not the final decision-maker — and closes with evidence the resolution actually held over time rather than quietly resurfacing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The specific case I had was actually the harder version of this — both units were disclaiming ownership of a shared product-reference data element, each saying it belonged to the other. Rather than picking one by authority, I traced which unit's process actually originates and most directly affects the data's accuracy, and in this case it was clearly the unit that first creates the product record, even though the other unit used it more heavily downstream. I made the cost of the current no-owner situation concrete and visible — I pulled together three recent examples where bad product data had caused real downstream problems, specifically so neither unit could treat 'nobody owns this' as a low-cost default. The unit that ended up with ownership wasn't thrilled, so I gave the other unit a formal consulted role in any future change to that data element's definition, so they weren't just overruled and walked away, they still had a real voice. Eighteen months later that ownership assignment has held, and when a dispute about a related field came up, both sides actually pointed back to that resolution as the precedent rather than reopening the whole argument.
commonMistakes: Resolves the dispute by escalating to authority/seniority rather than using a reasoned framework
Doesn't address the harder 'both units disclaim ownership' version of this problem
Doesn't make the cost of non-ownership concrete and visible to both sides
Leaves the losing side feeling overruled with no ongoing role, risking the resolution unraveling later
No evidence the resolution actually held over time
keyPoints: Uses a reasoned, non-arbitrary framework (proximity to the originating process) to assign ownership
Addresses the disclaimed-ownership case by making the cost of non-ownership concrete
Keeps the non-owning side genuinely engaged (e.g., a defined consulted role) rather than simply overruled
Provides evidence the resolution held over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses a sound, reasoned ownership-assignment framework
Addresses the disclaimed-ownership dynamic specifically
Keeps both sides genuinely engaged after resolution
Provides evidence the resolution held over time
